subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO WORLD SYSTEM OF SAMPLING RADIOACTIVITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet I might answer the question raised by the hon. member for Essex East yesterday as found at page 8590 of Hansard and which was in these words:
Is either hen. gentleman in a position to say whether or not all nations in the United Nations are now co-operating in the world wide attempt

to provide an adequate and accurate system of sampling radioactivity as a result of these explosions?
At the 14th session of the general assembly in 1959 an international program for the cooperative study of fall-out levels around the world was initiated as a result of Canadian leadership. Under that program countries which had the technical experience and the laboratory experience to carry out analyses of radioactive fall-out levels were asked to offer to countries not similarly equipped to undertake the analysis of samples collected in the territories of the latter in accordance with the program of work of UNSCEAR, the United Nations scientific committee on the effects of atomic radiation, of which Canada is an active member.
In addition to its active sponsorship of the resolution, Canada made an offer to carry out analyses of soil, food and bone samples collected in other countries. The governments of at least 14 other countries-I can name them if the hon. gentleman desires-as well as the international atomic energy agency and the world health organization have made similar offers. Accordingly, it is now possible for all countries in the world to obtain scientific data on the levels of radioactivity within their territories. Moreover, since 1959 there has been a marked increase in the number of member countries supplying UNSCEAR with data on radioactive levels.
Four countries, Burma, Malaya, Ghana and Pakistan, have so far indicated a desire to avail themselves of the Canadian offer, and the first samples collected m these countries are expected to be received in Canada shortly.

Mr. Chairman, when the house rose yesterday at six o'clock I had referred to the seriousness of the unemployment problem and had proceeded to deal with certain ideas that had been put forward to solve it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am having a little difficulty in hearing the hon. member because there is some undercurrent of conversation in the committee. I wonder if we could quieten down so the hon. member can receive a proper hearing.

I had pointed out that there are some who hold that the responsibility for providing jobs rests solely with the government, and with nobody else. I maintained
90205-6-545J
Supply-Labour
that this concept of making people employees of the state was not compatible with the concept of individual freedom, and that history had proven on more than one occasion that such a course leads only to dictatorship and tyranny.
There are some who feel that productivity is the answer. If we are going to examine this question I think we must ask ourselves exactly what we mean by productivity. If we mean an increase in over-all production, there is then some validity in this proposal. However, I think we must realize that its effectiveness will in large measure depend upon having markets for the increased production. We must also remember that productivity is synonymous with efficiency. We think of it in terms of more output per man hour. While this might improve our trading position and also the unemployment situation indirectly by enabling us to compete with foreign countries, both in our domestic markets and abroad, yet from this standpoint productivity is not likely to create many new jobs.
There are others who say that the answer to unemployment lies in greater emphasis on manufacturing, and particularly in expansion in the manufacturing of our primary products. I am sure this proposal will find a great deal of sympathy not only in this committee but throughout Canada, as manufacturing is lagging too far behind other industries in Canada. But here again we must realize the limitations of this proposal. It overlooks the handicap that we in Canada are under because our population is far too small to enable us to have the benefits of mass production. Hence an expansion in manufacturing can take place only behind a huge wall of tariff protection. This proposal also disregards our trading position. We produce many primary products which we cannot consume at home and which we must sell abroad. In order to sell abroad we must buy from other countries. This proposal also disregards the necessity for expanding the development of those areas which are dependent upon resource industries.
Still others have put forward the idea that the answer to our unemployment problem is increased capital investment, and probably this affords the best answer. But here also we must take account of the fact that if Canadians have the necessary capital, they are unwilling or reluctant to risk it in the development of our country. If Canadians will not provide the extra capital we require, we must be prepared to accept foreign capital and even to encourage it.
The truth is that there is no single cause of unemployment; therefore there is no single

Supply-Labour
cure. We must explore every avenue and exploit every opportunity to the fullest possible degree. While I said that government does not have all the responsibility for curing unemployment, that does not mean that government has not some responsibility. In fact government has a great deal of responsibility in this field, as many hon. members have pointed out. The chief responsibility of government to my mind is to create the kind of climate in which our free enterprise system can fulfil its normal functions. In order to do this the government has to provide proper incentives through sound fiscal and monetary policy. The government also has responsibility for providing wise and courageous leadership so as to inspire confidence at home and abroad; because while confidence may be something intangible it is nevertheless an important factor in helping to solve our unemployment problem.
The present government have already taken some measures to deal with our unemployment difficulties, and I wish to commend them most of all on their program of vocational training. I think we all realize that this is a long term program and that it cannot be expected to produce any immediate results. However, it is a necessary program, and no doubt it will bear fruit in due course. The government's retraining program will, perhaps, be less effective, because here we are dealing with people of an age where they are handicapped by mental attitudes which are not conducive to training of this kind. In many cases the men concerned are anchored to specific localities; everything they have is there, and they are unable to pull up their stakes and move elsewhere.
As far as the monetary policies of the government are concerned, the incentives so far have not proved effective in dealing with the problem in the underdeveloped areas of Canada. The figures for the Atlantic region referred to yesterday bear out this contention. Programs of public works are perhaps among the least effective measures which governments can undertake in order to alleviate unemployment. Only a few days ago I read an article in which it was pointed out that the Canso causeway cost around $23 million in public investment, yet provided jobs for only 150 to 200 persons. So much of our work today is done by mechanical means that this is the pattern we must expect. We shall not create the same ratio of jobs for public moneys out of public works projects as we might in other ways. This observation applies also to some extent to the winter works program. I very often feel that the winter works program looks better on paper than it really is.
Hear, hear.
Did you say "hooray"?

It reduces the number of unemployed for a specific period and makes the unemployment picture look better, but I feel that very often this is done at the expense of using up jobs which would become available later in the year in the normal course of events, when the work could be done more effectively and at lower cost to the taxpayer.
I think we should realize also that not only the government but industry has its share of responsibility with respect to unemployment. It seems to me that Canadian industry is too concerned with protecting capital investment and maintaining profits to play an effective role in solving this problem. I feel that Canadian industry is too prone to take the line of least resistance, to pass responsibility on to the government or to run to the government for protection whenever the going gets a bit hard. Industry in Canada must realize that freedom is only one side of the coin; the other side is responsibility. If freedom is lost, the capital investment and the dividends will go along with it. I think that contention has been borne out by what we have seen happening in Cuba, which is practically in our back yard.
Not only government and industry but labour as well must bear a full share of responsibility for seeking to solve this problem. In particular, labour has the responsibility of giving the maximum return for the wage dollar and for putting forward, whenever possible, ideas concerning ways in which management can effect savings and increase efficiency. In addition, labour has the responsibility for not making demands without having regard to the effect of such demands on other sectors of the population and on the economy as a whole. Certainly, both labour and management must realize that the welfare of each is bound up with the welfare of the other. They must learn to co-operate, because our country cannot afford a conflict between capital and labour. They must work together not only to prosper but to survive.
I think we all realize that we cannot solve this problem by pointing the finger at each other or by trying to fix the blame on each other. We must recognize that unemployment presents us with a tremendous problem and that "the fault is not in our stars" but in ourselves. No matter what measures are taken by the government, by industry or by labour, they will not work unless a determined effort is put forward to make them work. The human factor is all important, and we must

make a definite and determined effort to improve human relationships at all levels. Anyone who exploits difficulties in human relationships in order to cause friction is not only an enemy of Canada but an enemy of freedom.
Before I close I want to bring to the minister's attention once again a problem which I have already mentioned in this house on several occasions. If I remember correctly the minister promised that he would look into this, but my latest inquiries show that nothing has been done to date. I refer to the system by which government employees in the various maritime provinces are paid. I know that the minister's department maintains an office in St. John's where there is an employee who collects figures as to prevailing rates in different parts of the province. The rates paid by the government are based largely on the figures gathered by this employee on the advice he gets from the sources he consults.
I want to point out to the minister once again that the samples which this office collects are taken from too small an area. In fact I think we should not have differences of pay as between the maritime provinces, but that we should regard them as one single area and make the same rates of pay for government employees prevail throughout the whole Atlantic region. It seems to me preposterous that a person working on a ship, doing the same work as his colleagues and working in the same area, should receive less pay because, for example, he was recruited in Newfoundland. Yet men recruited in Newfoundland get one rate of pay, those recruited in Nova Scotia get another, and those recruited in Quebec get still another.
That situation prevails on the boats oper-rated by the hydrographic survey branch, on the icebreakers operated by the Department of Transport, and on other ships. These ships are doing the same work, are interchangeable and move from one area to the other. I feel there is a great injustice-one could almost call it discrimination-resulting from the system of prevailing rates which the government uses in calculating the wages of these employees. I urge the minister to take action with respect to this problem. I suggest that the only equitable way of dealing with it is to establish a standard scale of wages to apply throughout the whole maritime area.

Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member takes his seat I think it right that I should point out for the record that the problem of the rates of pay for Newfoundland seamen on Canadian government ships is now receiving active study and consideration, at least in the Department of Transport, with a view to having the rates
Supply-Labour
adjusted to put these men on a more equitable basis with their counterparts in the other maritime provinces.

I am glad to have that information from my hon. friend, but I wish to point out that in addition to the Department of Transport being involved the problem extends to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of Fisheries and even to the customs branch, which operates some ships. The problem is not confined only to people employed on the ships, but applies also to those who work in other fields. We should have a general policy for the maritime area with regard to government employees, under which we would give them equal pay for equal work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the course of his remarks on an earlier occasion in the discussion of this item the hon. member for Skeena introduced questions arising out of the wages paid prevailing rates employees in H.M.C. Dockyard, Halifax. It is well known that hon. members are occasionally required to be away from the chamber and that was my position when the hon. gentleman was speaking of these matters. I note that the hon. member who raised the subject has himself just been called from the chamber. It is ironic that while the hon. member was presenting the situation to the committee with something less than accuracy I was meeting with representatives of the Department of National Defence on the question. Because it is a matter that relates to the area represented in this chamber by the taller hon. member for Halifax and myself, I feel perhaps I should say a few words concerning it.
The question of the wages paid prevailing rates employees in H.M.C. Dockyard, Halifax, I suggest is not one which should be exacerbated by inaccuracies on the part of people who are not acquainted with the area nor fully knowledgeable with respect to the matter and, indeed, whose motivation might appear to be more related to a partisan attitude than one of true interest in the welfare of the workmen involved. There were major inaccuracies in the statement offered to the committee by the hon. member for Skeena.
I do not wish at any time to confine myself to a simple denial of inaccuracies emanating from an hon. gentleman who it perhaps would not be realistic to expect to be accurate.
I cannot refrain from commenting that it was a source of amazement to me that the hon. member for Skeena, British Columbia, should find it desirable to speak in this chamber about a problem that obtains at the other end of the country, when surely there are problems in the area from which he

Supply-Labour
comes to which he might more usefully attend. However, this is happily a free country, and it is wholly within the prerogative of any hon. member to raise in this chamber a matter of consequence to any constituency in Canada.
I do not deny the seriousness of the situation in the dockyard, but I feel I owe it to my constituents to place on the record a more accurate version of the situation, and perhaps hon. members of the committee will consider it useful that I do so. I might say that these facts are all known to the Minister of Labour whose estimates are now before us. Only 72 hours have elapsed since I last spoke to him about this question. The minister is personally familiar with the inaccurate references in which the hon. member for Skeena indulged.
For instance, the hon. gentleman said there have been occasional walkouts at the dockyard in Halifax. If this were true, and I hasten to say it is not, it would be a matter of concern to all hon. members, because the dockyard there is now the abode of two thirds of the ships, officers and men of the Eoyal Canadian Navy. At a time when hon. members of all parties have acknowledged the gravity of the international situation it would be a matter of consequence if workmen in this area were engaging in itinerant walkouts. There has been none at the dockyard.
1 am not suggesting that the workmen at the dockyard should be denied or should deny themselves any rights to which they feel entitled, but when a misstatement of fact has been made it requires immediate correction. The men have not walked out. Occasional union meetings have been held, but the men have not walked off the job in the dockyard. I for one, and my colleague from Halifax for another, are doing everything in our power to bring about a situation in which the men there will find it not in their interest to take steps of the kind referred to.
Among other things, the hon. gentleman said yesterday that there used to be an arrangement for starred rate differentials for extra skills. That arrangement still exists. Dockyard employees in certain trades and skills receive a starred differential of 5 cents an hour over shipyard rates.
The hon. member suggested that the interdepartmental committee meets in secret. The committee occasionally meets in Ottawa and has done so with increasing frequency in the last few weeks. It has to meet here in an effort to settle the employees' demands. Men are available to come to Ottawa at any time. Last evening I was speaking by long distance telephone to one of the representatives of the

employees. I have done this practically every day for the last ten days. They are available to come here and are anxious to co-operate in settling the matter. They were here three weeks ago and are eager to come again to any meeting which might be useful. The interdepartmental committee did not meet in secret when it met in Halifax. It met with representatives of the men and heard their wage demands.
What is the background of the current request of prevailing rates trades in H.M.C. Dockyard, Halifax, for an increase in wages? It was in the apparent interest of dockyard prevailing rates employees in the past to be identified for pay purposes with comparable trades in the private shipbuilding and repair industry. Although we have great confidence that the recent shipbuilding construction assistance program announced by the Minister of Transport will bring about a useful change in this area, over recent years it has been possible for contracting companies and their representatives to negotiate wage agreements with their employees that have been more favourable than those that have been negotiated by shipyards workers' representatives. So that historically in the past dockyard employees found it apparently in their interest to be identified with shipyard wages.
Now they do not. When it was in their interest they wanted to be identified with shipyard rates. Now that it is not in their apparent interest they do not want to be identified with shipyard rates. We can all understand this; we can all understand they would want to move to a higher wage level with which they could compare their wages. There is no secret about the prevailing rates policy. Essentially it means that prevailing rates employees in H.M.C. Dockyard, Halifax, are identified with comparable shipyards trades.
Well, as I have said, over a period of years in the past they found this in their interest. Now they do not; therefore they want to move away from it, but the government policy is to identify dockyard employees with shipyard rates. I point out that it does this not only in the Halifax dockyard but also in Esquimalt; therefore any change in this policy must be one that affects both Halifax and Esquimalt. It is understandable that the prevailing rates trades in H.M.C. Dockyard, Halifax, would want to move away from what they consider to be lower comparable shipyards rates. What they are asking for is a fundamental change in government policy.
The hon. member who spoke yesterday, the itinerant British Columbian who came in here with his inaccuracies, asserted that simply because the government has not immediately accepted the whole demand of the prevailing

rates employees it is procrastinating, nefarious, or doing something that is against the workers' interest. I venture the opinion that I am at least as well informed about the dockyard employees in the Halifax area as is the hon. member for Skeena. I had better be. 1 have met with them at times when they were drafting reports to government. I have talked to them on regular occasions in the dockyard, and I am in constant and daily communication with their representatives in the present circumstances.
The hon. member for Skeena did not find it possible yesterday to mention that the dockyard prevailing rate employees were just granted a 6 cents an hour increase, 3 cents of which was retroactive for a full 12 months. This 6 cents an hour increase did not satisfy the dockyard workers in Halifax. It did not satisfy them because it simply retained the adhesion of dockyard rates to shipyards rates. I understand that, but they have had a 6 cents increase as a way toward full justice. It is asserted that there is no apparent solution to the problem. The hon. gentleman said at page 8610 of Hansard:
No action has been taken toward a solution, nor is there any indication that a solution will be arrived at.
After the meeting with the workmen in Halifax, the interdepartmental committee reported last April to treasury board, and treasury board decided against the application of dockyard employees in Halifax for increased wages. This was disappointing to the workmen; in many instances it was inflammatory to them. That is not unreasonable with respect to men who apply for wage increases when they do not get them immediately, and do not get all of them. This does not mean that a workman can reasonably go out and accuse the man who refuses it of being a blackguard or a procrastinator. What happened was that the men did not satisfy treasury board of the adequacy of their case. There was no secrecy about the treasury board ruling in this matter.
I invited the representatives of the seven prevailing rates locals in H.M.C. Dockyard to come to Ottawa. They said they were prepared to do that and are now prepared to do it with responsible and reasonable action. I invited them to come to Ottawa and I personally told them of the treasury board decision and the reasons for it, in a room in this very House of Commons. As one of their two members I would have been glad to give them happier information; we would all be glad to see our people get wages higher than they are now getting. No member of parliament is going to turn it down. But they wanted an answer, and they received one. It was not
Supply-Labour
the one they wanted, but it was not procrastination. It was a judgment that they had not made their case, and they were given explicit reasons why treasury board had reached that decision.
The very next day, in my presence, those seven representatives of H.M.C. Dockyard, Halifax, were given a personal assurance by the Associate Minister of National Defence that when they appealed that ruling he would see that their appeal was reconsidered. They went away from here unsatisfied with the result of the treasury board hearing. They were disappointed with the result, but they were assured that they had access to appeal procedure.
What is unfair about that? They went back to Halifax and drafted an appeal and sent it to the Associate Minister of National Defence. Then two of them, Mr. Hayter and Mr. Lyons, came here from the N.D.E.A. conference in Montreal. Again they had a meeting with the Associate Minister of National Defence, which I arranged for them at their request. They were told by the minister that in his judgment this appeal would require at least until September 30 for full consideration by treasury board. There was no procrastination; there was no delay, and no deception was practised. There was an honourable statement by an honourable minister that it would take some time to handle the appeal, because it was a request to upset a ruling and to change a fundamental labour policy.
Well, it is not September 30 yet. In their wisdom the men have issued a statement that this is not the time to threaten the government; that the government will not act faster if it is under an ultimatum. In any event, the deadline of at least September 30 has not arrived. I am not the spokesman for treasury board. Treasury board did advise me, as it would advise any member of the house if he sought the information, which apparently the hon. member who spoke yesterday did not bother to do. They had a meeting last Thursday and gave initial consideration as a body to this wage appeal. They are still considering the matter and searching for a formula, perhaps not one that will satisfy all the demands of the workmen but one that will at least go part way toward doing so.
The workmen at H.M.C. Dockyard, Halifax, work in an area which is at the very heart of Canada's connection with the sea and with the men who sail the sea. Halifax was founded as a naval fortress. Its dockyard has been in existence for more than 200 years. When parts of this country were bald prairie, men worked on ships in the Halifax dockyard. These men, the descendants of Nova Scotia seamen and ship workers, in my opinion are not going to

allow unreasonable, unreasoning or misguided representation of their case in this house by others to deter them from their advocacy of higher wages in a reasonable, just and fair way.

I will be interested to learn during the course of discussion of these estimates what answers have been discovered, because there are many people in Canada who know something about this problem. I refer the minister to the excellent compilation of articles by Mr. J. Bascom St. John, which appeared in the Globe and Mail beginning on May 7, 1958. They have been published under the heading "Technical Education". I should like to read the foreword to that publication. The editor says:
In almost all western countries, the startling technological achievements of Soviet Russia have inspired a renewed interest in the quality and types of education available to our young people, especially in the technical field. Some controversy exists as to whether technical education in Ontario is fulfilling the expectations held forth when a need for it was first recognized about 60 years ago.
The concluding article in the series refers to the fact that this is a matter that has been given close attention in almost all modern European countries and in Great Britain following the Russian example. Under the chapter headed "Ontario Program Needs Reform" there is the following:
That something ought to be done is evident from the cost of technical education.
Many other excellent studies have been developed on this subject, and in this regard Britain leads the way. I have here a publication issued by the federation of British industries entitled "Further Education for Those in Industry and Commerce", which deals with this problem in some detail. We are familiar with the book "Technical Education and Social Change", published in Britain, and I quote the following from page 205:
Yet this study indicates the need for a radical rethinking of the system of further education in its relations to the social structure if the demands for trained manpower are to be met... Rapid change will require political action ...
We know there has been rapid change. Has there been any real political action? In the booklet-
What booklet are you holding? What do you call it?
I am holding a booklet- I am answering the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi-which is entitled "The Record Speaks".
Hear, hear.

This is a booklet which has a portrait of the Prime Minister on the front page over the name "Canada". Under the chapter headed "Labour" there is a paragraph which reads:
Canada is living in the midst of an automation revolution. While it will be beneficial in the long

Supply-Labour
run, nevertheless this revolution has caused part of the Canadian labour force to be unemployed.
We are well aware of this fact. I should like to touch on the record, and the way the record speaks, in so far as this administration is concerned. As I develop my thoughts with respect to the productivity council may I say this. Although we do not have the technical facilities that they have in Germany or western Europe, in Japan or in the United States, in Russia or in Great Britain, nevertheless we do have something with which to start namely people who care a great deal about this problem. In the town in which I live we have a man named Ardell Wilson who has done a great deal for technical training. If he received some encouragement at the official level this man could do a great deal for the young men who	have been	walking	our	streets
wishing that the plants would take on more employees. The people who are out of work have been longing for some kind of training in the interim period, and it has not been forthcoming.
In a part of Smiths Falls just north of my riding there is a technical school, called the trades	college of	Canada.	We	can beproud of this institution which is operated by Commander Clarence W. Warner. In talking to	Mr. Warner about	the	coursesthis college offers I discovered it offered courses in	television	electronics, industrial
electronics, refrigeration and air conditioning and automotive mechanics. Smiths Falls is a small place, and if it is possible to operate such a college there it is possible to do so elsewhere.
Commander Warner was in charge of operations of our radar school during world war II, one of the important electronic installations on the allied side. The commander is presenting a course of study which is available to men between the ages of 16 and 65. He is serving people who reside in Smiths Falls, and serving those outside of Smiths Falls by mail. You may be interested to learn, Mr. Chairman, that we have navy personnel in the Queen Charlotte islands, in Fort Churchill and elsewhere in Canada who are taking technical training at considerable expense to themselves, running between $400 and $500, in order that they will be better equipped to enter the employment field in Canada. Surely this sort of thing could be done under more spirited leadership than that which has been shown in the past few months.
Another matter I think I should mention is that we must be prepared to courageously, fearlessly, and in a non-political way review the Unemployment Insurance Act. There was

an address delivered on this subject by the member for Kingston prior to the summer adjournment and I am sure the contents of that speech are worthy of examination. There are many things that could be done here. We might separate one type of employee from another, always keeping in mind the proposition that people are our most important asset. There is nothing in Canada, capital, ores, lands, transportation, that is as important as the people we have here. This is our real source of wealth.
During the question period on September 20 last I ventured to ask a question of the Minister of Labour, as reported at page 8594 of Hansard for that date. I asked how many times the productivity council had met since its appointment on February 28, 1961, and had the government received any recommendations from the council. I was interrupted during the course of this question period and no answer was given. A number of members shouted, so there was no answer.
I hope there will be an answer to this rather important question, that is whether the productivity council, which was set up so long ago, has had any meetings that have been productive. If so, what has the result been in so far as this government is concerned? It would seem to me that although this council comes under the purview of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, it is of vital significance to any consideration of the labour department estimates. Let the minister at this time tell us in a fairly expansive fashion what the situation is in this regard. I hope this question will not be cut off.
Canadians were reading for many months addresses given by the governor of the Bank of Canada to various audiences he was invited to address. Questions were directed to the Minister of Finance in respect of the policy of the government in relation to the governor, and finally we had the fiasco that took place in the early part of this summer. I ask now if the minister would be kind enough to address himself to this question of the extent to which this ministry is in sympathy with the various addresses that have been given by representatives of this productivity council. There is an article in the Hamilton Spectator of June 7, 1961 in which Mr. H. George De Young is quoted as follows:
Most of our people have no conception of the seriousness of Canada's position.
Until we get a change in attitude we will continue to have those who wish to change the productivity council to gain factional goals.
He went on to say that Canada's gross national product per person has decreased since 1956 while that of most competing countries has gone ahead. Taking 1950 as 100 Mr. De

Young gave the following estimated figures for 1960, with those for 1956 in brackets. Canada 111 (116); the United Kingdom 124 (115); France 142 (125); Germany 185 (152); Italy 175 (135); the Netherlands 140 (127); Sweden 128 (115); Japan 190 (147). I say, Mr. Chairman, that this is an extremely serious matter and should be of concern to every member in this committee.
The same speaker, Mr. H. George De Young, gave an address on May 29, 1961 in which he said:
-Canadians will have to accept change if they are to help Canada move into the organized big league of world trade.
The other day I read into the record of Hansard a reference in the London Times to the arguments that have been advanced by our Minister of Finance and Minister of Trade and Commerce, in which those arguments were referred to as "negative" and "sterile". I would be curious to know what policy, if any, this Department of Labour has with respect to growth, with respect to economic policy. Has this government any economic policy at all?
If you have eyes to see and ears to hear, yes.
I am sorry; I missed the interruption by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi.
You did not miss anything.
He is just talking to himself.

The editor of the Quebec Chronicle-Telegraph, which is a fairly wise newspaper that has been sensitive to trade and industry in general, and whose editor knows a great deal about commercial conditions both in Great Britain and northwest Europe, had this to say:
Canada's Industrial might cannot remain prosperous if the market is restricted to 18 million people residing within our borders.
Is it the policy of this minister, as it appears to be the policy of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance, to be satisfied with things the way they are? We are not satisfied, Mr. Chairman, with the way things are at all. We enthusiastically support any steps this government may take with respect to putting young men in uniform and teaching them to dig shelters, and all that sort of thing, but conditions in the world are such that we feel this government is overlooking the real problem we have here. I refer to the problem of how this country is going to grow and assume its proper place in the wealth of nations.
Supply-Labour

I made a full and comprehensive statement on the function of the Department of Labour when the estimates of this department were up for consideration by the committee of supply of this House of Commons some time in March, when discussions on the estimates of this department were carried on for a full two days. On rising today it is not my intention to be belligerent in any way or to be critical of the remarks that have been made so far in this debate, but rather to put on the record certain pertinent facts with respect to the unemployment situation in Canada.
Controversy has arisen as to when the present unemployment situation actually started. I am not going to enter into the argument about that aspect of the matter, but I should like to read from the report of the special committee of the Senate on manpower and employment, at page 21. There we find the following statement:
With the wisdom of hindsight one can see in the statistical record evidence of weakness emerging gradually over a period of many years.
Here they were discussing the unemployment situation. I will deal with unemployment and indicate some of the measures that have been taken by the government to correct the situation.
Deal with them all.

I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that unemployment has taken a dramatic downturn in recent months. My opinion that the figures were considerably improved was confirmed when hon. members opposite failed to ask me any questions when the dominion bureau of statistics release was made the other day. This situation is quite understandable, but how different the attitude is when the figures show an increase in unemployment in this country. As a matter of fact, a decrease of 31,000 between the month of July and the month of August is not only greater than seasonal but is a record for all the years in which figures have been collected, and they have been collected since 1944. It is a record since 1944.
The hon. member for Essex East, in speaking on the estimates yesterday, said that in the report of the special committee of the Senate on manpower and employment it is stated that we must provide one million jobs in the next four or five years. I wish to bring to the attention of this committee the fact that this government is in the process of doing just that. Since 1957 during the term of office of this government more than half a million new jobs have been created in Canada.
In August unemployment represented 4.8 per cent of the labour force. This figure

Supply-Labour
trunk collector sewers, and agreed to write off 25 per cent of the loans covering work put into place before March 31, 1963. By September 5, loans amounting to $35.4 million had been approved for a total of 106 projects. I remind the committee that on September 7 last the Minister of Public Works introduced a resolution, now approved by the house, to amend the National Housing Act of 1954 in order to increase the amount of money available for all the undertakings I have mentioned.
In the field of industrial development, in order to encourage industries to locate in certain areas in Canada where unemployment has been chronic over the years we are allowing double depreciation for income tax purposes for such industries. The hon. member for Essex East made mention of this program, and minimized it. As hon. members of this committee are probably aware, it is the responsibility of the Department of Labour to receive applications from municipal authorities, to review the record of employment and unemployment in those localities, and to make recommendations to the government with respect to the designation of surplus manpower areas.
Applications for accelerated depreciation certificates from individual firms are dealt with by the Department of Trade and Commerce. This program is in two parts. If an industry wishes to produce a new product that has not as yet been produced in Canada it can locate in any area in Canada and be eligible for this double depreciation allowance. If an area makes application to be designated as a surplus manpower area and following the survey is so designated and qualifies under the formula, an industry locating in that area or municipality also qualifies for the allowance. Since publication in March of the regulations relating to the plan, applications have been received by the Department of Trade and Commerce covering a wide variety of products including chemicals, steel, textiles, electronics, plastics, food and other products. The value of the assets covered by these applications is approximately $85 million. It would appear that a representative cross section of Canadian secondary industry is taking advantage of the program, with some firms establishing new plants while others are enlarging their present facilities in order to manufacture new products and thus diversify their output.
The municipal authorities have shown a great deal of interest in this plan. They have become aware of the advantages attendant upon attracting new industries. By mid September of this year 49 applications had been received from various municipal and county authorities requesting designation under the

program. The government as at this stage has designated for the purposes of the program eight local areas administered by the national employment service. These areas included in their boundaries 16 of the municipalities and counties that applied for designation. In addition, 11 specific localities have been designated. The Department of Labour after investigation found that 17 of the areas that applied for designation could not qualify under the program at the present time. Investigation is presently continuing with respect to a further five applications.
I think it will be of interest to note that of the applications for accelerated depreciation that have been received by the Department of Trade and Commerce from individual firms, applications covering assets valued at $42 million were from firms intending to locate in surplus manpower areas. I submit that this program is working effectively and has brought about results. We have also provided an easement in the corporation tax for smaller firms. Canadian manufacturing will be further assisted through anti-dumping legislation in relation to "class or kind" goods made in Canada.
A national productivity council has been established by this government, and has been held up for ridicule by some people. The council has already met three times. I anticipate that the council will assist in the establishment of new industry, the development of a larger skilled labour force and the coordination of activities to increase productivity. I feel it will serve as a clearing house for information and ideas reaching down through the regional committees and committees which already exist in the industry.
Yesterday on the orders of the day the hon. member for Leeds asked a question in respect to this matter. Upon checking Hansard I find that in the first part of his question the hon. gentleman inquired how many times the productivity council has met since its appointment and whether it reported to the government. The productivity council will implement its own program. However, it may advise on the implementation of programs relating to productivity. At the next meeting, which is going to be held in Ottawa on Monday and Tuesday, September 25 and 26, I understand they will be considering labour-management co-operation services.
I must point out, Mr. Chairman, that the government has no control over the activities of the productivity council. We have established this council, and its membership consists of some outstanding Canadians representing every segment of our economy. They are on their own, and we expect they will be

bringing a great deal of benefit to industry and the economy as a whole in the months and the years to come.
One of the most significant programs administered in my department has been the municipal winter works incentive program, a program that the hon. member for Essex East refers to as a bagatelle.
Anaemic, I said.
The municipal winter works program has proved an effective method of stimulating employment at the local level during the time when seasonal unemployment is at its peak.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the minister, but his time has expired.

Under ordinary circumstances the committee would want the minister to go on; especially is this so because of his generous treatment of the member for Essex East yesterday. I hope he will continue to be generous in his references to the member for Essex East, rather than severe in his indictment as he is being now.

I want to thank the hon. member for Essex East and the members of the committee for this opportunity to carry on. I wish to assure the hon. member for Essex East that I have no intention of being severe with him, or of being critical. What I am trying to do is to set the record straight.
This program has been in operation now for three winters. During the three winters of its operation a total of 12,127 applications has been approved by the provinces and accepted by the government of Canada. The total cost of work put in motion during the three winters is estimated to be over $500 million, of which it is estimated over $350 million was expanded during the period covered by the three programs. An estimated 214,440 jobs have been provided over the three winters. The number of man days of work provided is estimated to be 8,812,394.
This program for the coming winter has been broadened to quite an extent to include almost any municipal undertaking of a capital nature, and it is expected that next winter's program will be even larger than that of last winter. Under the public works sector we have had an ambitious program of public works, and this has been pushed forward during the past three years. As an example, the Department of Public Works has in progress at various points across this country some 19 architectural projects each valued at more than $1 million. There are many who maintain that the government
Supply-Labour
should launch upon a very large public works program. That is exactly what we are doing, Mr. Chairman.
In addition to this, six architectural projects valued at between $500,000 and $1 million are under contract. There are also 16 engineering projects, each valued at more than $500,000, in progress at this time. The expanded program of public works had in 1958, 50 architectural projects under way each with a value of more than $1 million, and 33 engineering projects with a value of more than $500,000 each.
We are now carrying out a program of engineering and maintenance projects which are worth well over $400 million. These include a $13 million harbour improvement at St. John's, Newfoundland; construction of the new $22 million aeroquay at Malton airport in Toronto; construction of a $60 million power reactor at Kincardine, Ontario; the $35 million Champlain bridge at Montreal; defence construction contracts with a total value of $100 million; and projects with a total value of nearly $30 million being carried out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for other governmental departments and agencies.
I come now to the trans-Canada highway system. This program has been an encouraging one. In 1960 the Trans-Canada Highway Act was amended to provide an additional $50 million for construction and to extend the act until December 31, 1963. A great deal of work has been provided in this area.
In the resources development area the federal government, during the past four winters, has contributed half the cost of the $13 million program for the construction of camp grounds and picnic areas, and this work has provided some 650,000 man days of employment. Approximately $6 million is being spent this year-that is, in the fiscal year 1961-62-on national parks and historic sites. Another $2 million is being contributed over a period of four or five years toward the cost of camp sites and picnic grounds along the route of the trans-Canada highway, with the provinces matching this expenditure.
We are contributing half the cost of constructing roads that will open new areas for development, to a maximum of $7.5 million per province. When fully implemented this program will produce some 4,500 miles of roads to resources. Some 3,500 miles are under construction, and expenditures to date in all provinces total some $55 million, of which the federal government contributes 50 per cent.

Supply-Labour
The Columbia river power treaty, which was recently signed in Washington, provides, I submit to you, sir, the basis tor a very large expansion in that area also.
This is nonexistent. This is an amazing statement.
I said the treaty had been signed in Washington.
Signing a treaty does not give men work.

The Pine Point railway project, designed to tap new resources of mineral wealth, will involve a capital expenditure of at least $65 million on the new line alone, plus additional expenditures on line improvements south of Grimshaw. A new northern Quebec railway to Mattagami lake will open the way to further resources in this part of the province. Work on the South Saskatchewan dam is well ahead of schedule and is providing an important stimulus to this part of the west.
During the past four years this government has provided a $29.5 million loan to New Brunswick for the Beechwood hydroelectric development, and has made payments totalling $14.7 million to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick for terminal stations and 562 miles of transmission lines used in the interprovincial power grid system.
Some 2,300 miles of development roads are being constructed in Canada's northern territories, and 458 miles of low standard roads are being reconstructed to the development road standard at a total cost of $106 million. Development road construction has been completed on 574 miles, with 790 miles of right of way cleared. Some 800 miles remain to be surveyed. The forest access roads and trails agreement provided many jobs and expenditures in that area.
As far as small businesses are concerned, on January 19 of this year the Small Business Loans Act came into effect. By way of a guarantee of loans made by banks, it provides intermediate and short term credit to proprietors of small enterprises for the improvement and modernization of equipment and premises. The government is now authorized to guarantee loans up to $25,000 and for periods up to 10 years. Up to the end of June 1, there were approved 394 loans with a total value of $10,484,275. However, small business organizations have estimated that the value of renovation and extension work waiting to be carried out under this act amounts to $75 million. The government has also provided an easement of corporation taxes.
As far as trade stimulation is concerned, this is very vital to our economy from the

point of view of supplying jobs. In the automobile industry, for example, the excise tax on cars was abolished.
Thanks to our efforts.

I promised the hon. member that I would not enter into any controversy with him so I am not going to make any attempt to reply to what he has just said. We have also taken action with respect to the discount on imported motor vehicles and parts through reduction of the discount allowed. We have taken steps to make foreign automobile manufacturers compete on more equal terms with Canadian manufacturers. Meanwhile the recommendations of the royal commission on the automobile industry are being considered.
Would the minister permit me to ask him one question for clarification? He talked about foreign cars competing more equally with Canadian cars. Among foreign cars does he include British cars?
All cars that are imported into Canada are designated as foreign cars, and I think the hon. member for Essex East will agree with me on that.

You and I can
agree on that subject.

Our merchandise trade deficit, which has been a source of great concern to all of us, was reduced in 1960 to $97 million from $369 million in 1959. In 1956, for example, our trade deficit was $713 million and I repeat that in 1960 it was reduced to $97 million. I feel that this gives reason for satisfaction. The employment benefits from this reduction are going to be significant, and a further reduction in our trade deficit is being attempted.
We have endeavoured to help and give leadership to Canadian businessmen interested in developing further trade abroad. Recently we arranged to bring the trade commissioners to Ottawa so that they might meet those who are in business in this country. The conference proved to be very successful and some 1,400 business executives took advanage of it. It was significant to find at that time that about 20 per cent of the businessmen attending these meetings were for the first time considering the development of an export market for their goods.
To enable Canadian business to compete on better terms in foreign markets, the government provides assistance through the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. This assistance has been expanded and the results are gratifying because we are able to ship more goods made in Canada through the facilities

oi this corporation as well as through the Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited.
I turn now to the field of training which has been a source of interest to a great many people including members of the government party, the government itself and members of the opposition. I want to remind the committee that as a result of the act passed by the house before Christmas a new federal-provincial agreement became effective on April 1, 1961. This agreement provides for a greatly increased technical and vocational program in Canada. The objective of the new agreement is to provide a means whereby Canada's manpower training requirements may be met. In the new agreement emphasis is placed on upgrading and retraining those now employed as well as on pre-employment training for those entering the work force.
The number of unemployed persons receiving training has increased each year and a substantial increase is expected during the coming winter. In his remarks yesterday the hon. member for Essex East referred to this act and said that it was not meeting the need for training the unemployed because grade 10 education was required and also because the act does not provide for training in academic subjects. He also said that the act requires amendment to correct this situation. Neither the act nor the agreements require grade 10 education for entry into the unemployed training courses. The normal entrance requirements have been waived for most courses except where a knowledge of advanced mathematics is necessary for successful mastery of the courses.
The vast majority of the numbers of unemployed being trained have formal education much below grade 10 level. Basic training in mathematics, science and communication skills necessary to obtain and hold employment has become an integral part of the training program for the unemployed in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Quebec and New Brunswick. Plans are now being made to operate such courses in all provinces during the present fiscal year. However, the act does not require amendment to meet the problem referred to by the hon. member for Essex East.
In his remarks a few moments ago the hon. member for Leeds mentioned the inadequacy of training in the technical field. I am unable to recollect the figures he used but for his information I wish to advise him that in the year 1960-61 training in technical and vocational classes in institutions throughout the country was given on a continuing basis to some 368,347 Canadians so the fact is that there are people being trained on a continuing basis in institutions established for this purpose. The hon. member may have had in
Supply-Labour
mind the short courses that are established for some specific purpose and for a limited time, with the federal government paying 75 per cent of the cost. When these people are trained these courses are, of course, discontinued, but the fact is that some 368,347 people were being trained across Canada in the year 1960-61. We have not got the figures for 1961-62.
The hon. member also mentioned that technical people are leaving this country in increasing numbers. I was interested in reading an article published in the Montreal Gazette today. It is headed, "Skilled Personnel Return". I think it is important enough that I should read a portion of what is said here because all of us are very much interested in this matter. The article reads in part as follows:
A small but growing return to Canada of Canadian professional and technical personnel has been remarked by the technical service council, an industry sponsored placement agency which has opened an office in Montreal. The annual exodus of Canadian trained scientists and engineers still greatly exceeds the numbers who are returning, and no doubt will continue to do so for some time yet. Still, it is encouraging to know that the traffic is no longer so obviously one way.
The causes for a return to Canada are several. They arise, for the most part, from a dissatisfaction with the American way of life. A related consideration is the readiness with which many American employers will lay off even skilled personnel when times are bad. Canadian firms, in the experience of the council, tend to hold on to their men; American firms do not.
The council does not appear to have experienced much difficulty in placing the returnees. An encouraging demand is developing for professional personnel in anticipation of improved business activity.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us the source of this information?

The Montreal Gazette of Thursday, September 21, an article on page 12 written by John Meyer, the financial editor. I continue the quotation:
The demand for production engineers, time study and cost experts is particularly significant. It suggests to the council further evidence of Canadian producers' sharpening awareness of the need to wring out cost consuming slack in their operations.
There may be another reason for the reported views of a number of these technical people, and that may be that they have found out this government has taken action and that the economy of Canada is on the upward swing, that opportunities are here again.
Now, I should like to make a statement on the training program in so far as facilities and the equipment of those facilities are concerned. As a result of the stimulus of increased federal contributions to training provided in the new technical and vocational

Supply-Labour
training bill passed earlier this session, additional expenditures on new and enlarged training facilities are now planned by the provincial governments amounting to $164,808,000 up to March 31, 1963. This is the program that provincial governments have indicated in so far as these facilities are concerned. The federal government will contribute 75 per cent of this total expenditure, and we have already approved an amount of $98,312,000 as our share.
The province of Quebec signed the training agreement last Friday afternoon, following similar action by all the other provinces earlier. Applications for approval from Quebec are expected1 shortly. All the provinces have signed the necessary agreements. The Quebec program will add to the totals I have given.
Of the $98 million which the federal government has already approved for capital expenditures, it is expected that $62 million will be claimed during the present fiscal year. There will probably be another $4 million or $5 million from Quebec. Provision is made in the present estimates for capital expenditures by the federal government of $29,500,000, of which sum $15 million is in the main estimates and the balance in the supplementary estimates. I anticipate, Mr. Chairman, that there will be need for an additional amount to be provided in a later supplementary estimate to cover the remainder.
Included in the new facilities that have already been approved are nine institutes of technology, 11 trade schools, 69 vocational high schools, making a total of 89 new technical and vocational training institutes across this country. Now, these facilities and the enlargement of the existing schools will, it is estimated, provide accommodation for an additional 30,000 students. I submit this is a very worth-while program which has been given life by the federal government and which provides an incentive to the provinces to undertake these worth-while projects.
In the field of transportation, I would recall to hon. members that during the past three years over $45 million were spent in providing new and modern ships for the Department of Transport. Other ships have been built by the federal government to be operated by other bodies such as the Canadian National Railways, and this work brings the total expenditure in the field to $57 million. The ship construction assistance regulations went into effect on September 12. These regulations provide for a subsidy in respect of construction in Canada of self-propelled vessels of 100 tons or over, tugs of 50 tons or over and other vessels of 200 tons or over. This, too, Mr. Chairman, I submit will give the

necessary boost to the shipbuilding industry of our country which has suffered in the past.
In the field of winter employment, the federal government has taken an active interest in trying to stimulate co-operation between all Canadians across this country to provide more employment during the months in which it is most needed. All of these programs, and these are only some of the programs I have time to bring to the attention of this committee, were brought forward by this government for the purpose of stimulating planned investment, to create new jobs and guarantee old jobs and to maintain a healthy degree of expansion of the economy. These things are now taking place.
What has been the result of this action by the government? The gross national product was up 3 per cent in the second quarter of 1961 over the second quarter of 1960; personal expenditures on goods and services were up 3.8 per cent. Government expenditures on goods and services were up 7.9 per cent. Exports of goods and services were up 9.7 per cent. Wages and salaries were up by 3.5 per cent. In the field of employment, total employment, at 6,381,000, was up 110,000 from August, 1960. There were 59,000 more men and 51,000 more women employed in August, 1961 than a year ago. There were
5.578.000	employed in non-farm industries,
127.000	more than in August, 1960. There were 803,000 employed on farms, and this figure dropped by 17,000 as compared with a year ago. Manufacturing employment was up 41,000 from August, 1960; wholesale, retail trade employment was up 24,000; finance, insurance and real estate employment was up 14,000; and there were 68,000 more people working in the service industries than there were a year ago.
I should give the committee the regional picture in so far as employment is concerned. On a regional basis, employment in the Atlantic region was up by 32,000; the Quebec region was down 29,000; the Ontario region up 59,000; the prairie region up 26,000; the Pacific region up 22,000. In so far as the percentage of unemployment is concerned as related to the labour force of these regions, the Atlantic region, 6.8 per cent as against 6.9 per cent in August, 1960; in Quebec it is now 6.3 as against 6.2 per cent; in Ontario it is 3.9 per cent as compared with 5.1 per cent last year at this time. In the prairies, it is 2.7 per cent as compared with 2.4 per cent last year and in the Pacific region it is 6.3 per cent as compared with 7.5 per cent last year. I am sorry to have taken up so much of the time of this committee, Mr. Chairman, but I felt that some of these things had to be brought to the attention of this

committee, in order that all of us may realize that no effort has been spared by this government to deal with this unemployment situation in Canada. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I can assure the members of the committee and the people of Canada that this government will continue to exert all possible effort on behalf of the Canadian economy and the Canadian people as a whole.
Mr. Chairman-
