speechtext: I understood that, following a government member, it is normally the turn of some member of the opposition. I do not wish to dispute the right of the hon. member for Peterborough, of course, if that has been the practice.

I am
informed that the hon. member for Leeds spoke prior to the minister and the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont prior to him. I therefore believe it is in order for one of the members of the C.C.F. party to have the floor. I recognize the hon. member for Laurier next.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. What we have seen happen here this afternoon is, I think, rather extraordinary. We have had virtually a speech from the throne in reverse. We have had the citation at the end of the session of all the actions of the government over the last seven or eight months, and this is quite an innovation I am sure. However, I feel there are one or two things which were stated by the Minister of Labour which should not pass unnoticed. One of the things which always interests me is the rather interesting logic behind such statements. I can remember last December and January, when we saw these figures rising dramatically, the reason given for unemployment was loss of trade, the fact that the devastation in Europe had been repaired, that there was no longer any war scare and the fact that so many young people had entered the labour market and that the government had little part in it at all. But now that the figures are beginning to go down, suddenly the government's achievements are the main reason for it.
I was a little bit worried about the rationale which the Minister of Labour used in indicating that now 5 per cent is going to be looked upon as an acceptable proportion of unemployed. I can remember when, 10 or 15 years ago, a figure of 3 per cent was looked upon with concern and 4 per cent 90205-6-546
Supply-Labour
with great alarm. However, I believe now we are going to be expected to recognize 5 per cent.
No.

I would suggest that slight inflation can easily be looked after by an entirely planned economy and there will be no need to worry about that matter in terms of 5 per cent. Indeed, we must bring this unemployment figure further down than such a level.
One suggestion which I found somewhat surprising was the suggestion of the Minister of Labour that the hon. member for Essex East had misled this committee because he asserted that Canada had the highest unemployment rate of any country in the western world. The minister used the figures of June, July and August in order to prove this statement. I think that is a rather unfair example as Canada, of course, has a much greater fluctuation from winter to summer than has the United States. Surely the only fair way in which to decide this question would be to use both winter and summer figures in order to make any kind of acceptable comparison.
So far as the use of housing is concerned, I would think there may well be a serpent in the basket in the use of housing as a means of bringing down unemployment in this manner because, to my way of thinking, at a time when we are bringing down the income needed to buy a home, and when we are making mortgages with longer terms and payments much higher, if there is a slight recession there is going to be a tremendous number of houses which are going to be in the hands of the government. The government will be really in the housing business. What we need is direct action by the government in subsidizing low cost housing. One critic has suggested that the number of housing units is outpacing family formation in the middle income area and that this is going to be a real problem in the future.
Finally, the Minister of Labour indicated that the hon. member for Essex East had minimized the government's double depreciation measure. I would suggest that he could not possibly minimize it or it would disappear altogether, certainly in one aspect at least. So far as areas designated as surplus manpower are concerned, the minister did not prove that one single job was created by this particular piece of legislation. So far as areas being designated are concerned, this may look to be very strange at the moment, but certainly in the past we did not get any great run on this particular kind of help. In fact, it took from December until March before we could find out what the system was

Supply-Labour
going to be. Then, of course, by the time we finally found out what the system was going to be, we found that the measure was not strong enough to cure even the mildest form of unemployment. It was coming too late. There was no knowledge of it until March
2.	It was too late to do anything about the level of unemployment we had last winter, and of course, many knew nothing about it. I would suggest that the way in which this particular aspect of the government's policy has been handled has been the most complete negation of government responsibility which I think could possibly be examined.
The criteria were made fully public on March 2, but cities throughout the country had no idea whatsoever whether or not they were covered by these criteria. For example, in April or May I went down to the library to discover just exactly what the situation was in many areas of Canada. I found that so far as the metropolitan area of Windsor-Leamington was concerned, the figure was 80.9 per cent of the months between May and November between 1953 and 1960 and this city had applied. But when we turn to major industrial areas of 10,000 or more, which required 75 per cent, we find Rouyn-Val d'Or with a figure of 76.2 per cent had not applied; Shawinigan Falls with 90.5 per cent had not applied; Cornwall with a figure of 80.9 per cent had applied; Lac St. Jean with a figure of 76.2 per cent had not applied; Trois Rivieres with a figure of 90.5 per cent had not applied; Brantford with a figure of 90.5 per cent had not applied. Surely it would have been very simple for this government to inform the municipalities throughout this country at least to what extent they apply, in one of the areas which could come under this scheme.
I realize that, in order to find out whether the number leaving the industrial force was the reason for the number becoming less, certainly there was needed some kind of local investigation. I know of one community where the mayor came all the way down to Ottawa -and perhaps there were many others-when there was no possibility that that city could be given this designation of a surplus manpower area under this piece of legislation. This is government irresponsibility at its worst. If you go into most industrial areas of
10,000	and less what do you find? In those nine major industrial areas, eight had not applied. The minor industrial areas required 50 per cent. In St. Stephen the figure was 73.8 and it had not applied; Gaspe with 66.7 per cent had not applied; Rimouski with 61.9 per cent had not applied. Similarly I could go on down the list. This measure was supposedly to deal with unemployment at the time when there was unemployment which was, of

course, last winter. Now with employment rising the whole manner of government appreciation now with the very little effect it will have, almost becomes irrelevant. I think this is certainly a damaging indictment of a so-called method by which this government was going to deal with unemployment.
I am not going to comment on the mass of statistics which we have just been given. I am sure that all of us want to sit down for a few hours in order to read that speech before we can decide really what has been said. However, I wish to say this, at any rate, about this whole area of employment. Today, with all the seriousness of the international situation and with the bureau of statistics giving us at least a little bit more hope than it has given us in the past, perhaps unemployment does not seem to be quite so overwhelmingly significant. Perhaps this provides an opportunity to sit back more coolly and impassively and to discuss the problem of unemployment without the white heat of urgency we felt last March. We in the New Democratic party look upon this problem as the most serious of all the internal difficulties facing the people of Canada. The Senate committee put it very well when they indicated the extent of the material loss involved in unemployment. I am reading from page 1 of the report of the special committee of the Senate on manpower and employment wherein it is stated:
The failure of the economy to utilize fully its labour resources involves a loss of production. Nor can this production be later recovered-it is gone forever. Unemployment implies, then, both the inability of certain members of the society to share equitably in the national output and a reduction of the national output itself. Furthermore, the mere awareness that a significant number of people are out of work-and with the modern development of statistics and the means of communicating them widespread awareness is never long delayed-has an adverse effect on social morale and the climate of enterprise. In fact, the number of people without jobs is one of the most common and most important standards used to evaluate the performance of a free society and in the present world of ideological conflict it is hardly an overstatement to say that a high level of employment is a goal deserving of the utmost priority.
These are the material losses. Now we all hope that the cold war will soon be something of the past, but let us not forget that we shall have another war, though a different kind of war, on our hands, and the way in which we deal with unemployment will be a very real part of that war.
I should like to mention here the spiritual significance of unemployment. Lord Beveridge in his book entitled "Full Employment in a Free Society" says:
The greatest evil of unemployment is not physical but moral, not the want which it may bring but the hatred and fear which it breeds.

We on this side fully recognize that this is an extremely complex problem and that it has as many facets to its solution as there are to its causes. But there are two approaches. One is simply to stand back and say: we can do virtually nothing about it-at least in those circumstances the Canadian citizen knows just what to expect-and the other is to refuse blindly to accept the extent of the problem. This certainly was the policy of the present government through November, December and January of last year. Their philosophy was: we can spend a little money, take the minimum of action accompanied by the maximum of publicity, and hope that the Canadian people will be hoodwinked into believing that we have a policy of full employment. We in the New Democratic party have decided to hit this problem head on, much to the consternation of certain organizations. We say that a government must guarantee employment, using as its methods a wide range of fiscal, monetary and economic policies. This could be done, and we say it has to be done. We believe that we, in Canada, are the ones who are out of step with our slogans of "free enterprise". Let us look at what some of the other nations have done. I should like to quote from an address given by Mr. T. Carlsson, a Swedish labour attache to Canada and the United States in which he said:
Sweden controls its economy by exercising overall planning and integration of all phases of industry. No move is made in any one sector of the economy without regard to the effect on the country as a whole. When a recession threatens, the machinery to avert it is ready to swing into action immediately.
This, of course, is very different from the philosophy here where we wait until a man falls flat on his face and then pick him up, as distinct from doing something to bolster him before he falls.
Mr. Carlsson continued:
As a result of advance planning, the government and municipalities have public works projects ready to roll in an emergency to provide more jobs and stimulate the economy.
Private investment is encouraged in a recession by making it tax free for a limited period, thus developing new industry and expansion of existing facilities when it is most vitally needed.
And here, I think, is the important statement.
We don't tolerate unemployment in Sweden. A full employment policy is in the bedrock of our national economic system.
How do they maintain jobs for all in Sweden? The answer, again, lies in planning. To quote Mr. Carlsson again:
The workers in Sweden, including the white collar workers, are 95 per cent organized, and the employers are also fully organized. This makes it possible for the leaders of both unions and management to negotiate "economy-wide" contracts, governing every company and every 90205-6-546*
Supply-Labour
worker in the country. The profits of all companies are published periodically, and wages are geared scientifically to productivity.
Our employers have accepted their social responsibility. They acknowledge the right of the workers to share in their profits.
Then, later:
Labour mobility-the shifting of workers from one region to another and one trade to another- is a big factor in the Swedish success story. The government provides very generous travel allowances for families changing jobs, and offers vocational retraining courses of up to two years' duration-families being supported by government funds while the breadwinners learn a new trade.
You are a bore.
I am afraid the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi is in jocular mood this afternoon. I did not hear what the question was.
He is talking to himself.

I put it to the committee that another country has done something about unemployment. I have here a clipping from the Globe and Mail on June 9, 1961 headed: "West German Jobless Dues Suspended". Instead of the bankruptcy which virtually faces our own fund, Germany is in effect having to give a rebate to the workers who are being asked not to contribute further to the fund because it is already far too large.
The French economist, Andre Philip, speaking at a conference in August, 1961, said that in France "If we had 2 per cent unemployment we would have a revolution". Mr. Philip is further reported as saying:
In the European community we are changing our economic and social structure. In the United States and Canada you must also make a change because if you don't you will lose and you will make us lose, which I don't like.
We might well consider the position of New Zealand. Perhaps I could illustrate it by quoting from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of January 26 of this year.
New Zealand in fact seems a Fabian paradise, an almost classless society with full employment and high living standards. This little country of 2,300,000 has virtually no unemployment. Of a total labour force of 885,000, only 276 are registered as jobless. And at least 17,000 jobs are vacant.
Thus, governments abroad have realized that full employment is the only solution- full employment not merely as the subject of election speeches, but full employment in reality. We face the realization that we have today what is known as cyclical unemployment and that the cycle has changed. I am sure that is part of the reason for some of the more hopeful statistics we have heard from the minister. While we know that after a certain time cyclical unemployment seems to disappear, we should also recognize that it leaves behind a hard core

Supply-Labour
of men and women who do not re-enter the labour force. This hard core will cost the Canadian taxpayer a great deal more in the future. I am thinking of a piece of research which was done by the Catholic Service Bureau in my constituency. They examined the histories of people who are known as "down and outs"- those who sit on park benches and have lost all interest and participation in competitive living. The bureau's investigators found that nearly every one of those was a man who had had a job in his early thirties or forties, had lost that job and failed to re-enter the labour force. This constitutes a serious social problem and one which will cost even more than we are paying now in unemployment relief.
We realize that automation offers us an opportunity to increase the prosperity and living standards of the people of Canada, yet we stand wondering who is going to pay for this technical change-and we cannot help asking ourselves whether it is not going to be the workers who find themselves faced directly with the prospect of losing their jobs in an economy where they would find it difficult to find any other employment. We wonder, also, what would happen if the dream of total disarmament did come true. Could we reorganize our economy sufficiently to take up the slack and provide new employment for those now employed in the defence industries? I suggest that the government would have to take a far more conscientious view of its activities and responsibilities before there would be any hope that such a thing could happen. We believe there is a need for government responsibility. We were shocked by the lackadaisical attitude in dealing with the situation. We believe that the twentieth century makes great demands that call for some faith in democratic government action. I am sure that future historians in looking back at our age will not be so much impressed by our cars or even our missiles as by the fact that with the height of technological and scientific advance we have achieved our society was unable to give jobs to those Canadians who last winter were looking for employment, and will be even more impressed by our utter callousness in dealing with the situation.
Yesterday the hon. member for Essex East placed before the committee the program of the Liberal party for dealing with unemployment. We are able to agree entirely with many and indeed most of the points he raised. There was, however, one fatal flaw, almost Shakespearean in its depth.
Oh, the hon. member reads Shakespeare too.

The hon. member appeared to fail to realize that such activity, if it is to be co-ordinated and purposeful, demands a level of government participation and direction beyond that acceptable by the members and supporters of the Liberal party. We feel that success is impossible without a planned course, that all these principles would result in utter chaos. We are unhappy to see the word "planning" being dropped from the vocabulary of hon. members of the Liberal party.
I used it yesterday, but in the right context.

It is evident that the hon. gentleman and I disagree as to the meaning of the word and the proper context in which it should be used.
Without planning, many of these courses of action could lead to total chaos and confusion. We feel that the programs which appear so acceptable on the floor of the convention when the Liberals meet lose all shape and meaning once they are taken over by the party leadership.
We in this group also wish to present to the committee a program for dealing with unemployment. We believe that there must be a planned approach at every level. It will not be regimented and will be acceptable to the Canadian people. A planned approach is today used by captains of industry but without the full view being taken into consideration, without sufficient research and information, and all too often it entails planned profits and planned obsolescence. We wish to create a pattern within our economy which will provide a full employment society. By whom would it be planned? Certainly there would be an inner council of the cabinet. This is not a matter that should be the full responsibility of the Minister of Labour. Both the hon. member for Leeds and the hon. member for Essex East commented on this point as well. We envisage an inner council of the cabinet which council would be composed of the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and perhaps other appropriate ministers who would hammer out policies destined to bring about full employment in our society.
We would require a planned approach at the provincial level as well. We shudder at the course of this government at the present time. It is losing fiscal control in the new taxation arrangements with the provincial governments. We have a situation in which one province can negate the influence of the federal government. We had a classic example of that recently. The federal government

removed the tax on automobiles and the Ontario government introduced a 3 per cent sales tax.
What about the tax in Saskatchewan? We have had it for 20 years under a socialist government.
I suggest it was not levied in a manner similar to that in the instance to which I refer, nor by the existing government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It was increased by the C.C.F.
I am not attempting to discuss the irrelevant situation in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member had better talk about something he knows something about, if there be such a subject.

We require a planning and development council to dovetail plans and programs at every level. There must also be planning by different economic groups including industry, labour, agriculture, the extractive industries and others. These should be given a genuine role to play and not just sent away immediately after being constituted. They should have a genuine opportunity of participation, a sense of responsibility, an opportunity of following through and of making a vital contribution. They should not simply hold conferences. It is only through planning at the federal and provincial levels and at the level of all economic groups that we can possibly solve the problems with which we are confronted.
We wish to institute a program to give Canada the opportunity for the economic growth that is necessary to ensure her prosperity. This is the touchstone, as was mentioned by other hon. members who have participated in this debate. We must ensure that all sectors, regions and groups share in this growth and it must be a purposeful growth. It is all very well to talk about training the unemployed which is of course a necessary and important thing but if jobs were available industry would train men to fill the jobs. I have been told by industrial leaders that that is true. Certainly we need vocational training but it will not solve the problem. To achieve the purposeful sense of growth to which I refer we must come to appreciate that if one region is depressed and is not receiving a fair share of the national income we are all at fault, we all lose and that this is a measure of our failure to cope with our problem. If one group, whether it be old age pensioners, farmers or fishermen, is not receiving a just share of the national prosperity, we are all the losers and again we share responsibility for this failure.
We require a national investment board capable of implementing a dynamic investment policy and of planning and regulating
Supply-Labour
investment. It must direct this investment in a way that will create employment. Let us put a sense of purpose in our war on unemployment just as in times of emergency we have put a sense of purpose in our war against enemies when they have beset us. If we had that sense of purpose the Canadian people would rise to the occasion and invest their money in Canadian enterprise but lacking that sense of purpose there is no great desire to do so.
We need greater control over anti-cyclical financing as was mentioned in earlier discussions on the budget. This government has failed to adopt methods by which we can prevent recessions through the use of fiscal and monetary policy. This is a very real failure. There must be a recognition of the public sector, so long neglected. It must be appreciated that we can stop unemployment by building the schools, universities, recreational centres and other things we need. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Labour stress the importance of construction in relation to employment. The Minister of Public Works denounced us as being unrealistic when we said that public works could provide employment. There appears to be a difference of opinion on this matter within the ranks of the cabinet.
We require a new approach to secondary industry. We need a minister of industry. We have ministers for such departments as fisheries and mining and technical surveys. Secondary industry employs more people than any other segment of the economy and requires the establishment of a department with a minister to look after the many needs, obtaining there.
There are many other areas where a new approach must be adopted including that of area redevelopment. Redevelopment projects would aid in giving the Canadian people a sense of national purpose especially in areas where the economy loses its strength by reason of the relocation of industry or changes in technology. I refer to communities such as mining and industrial communities who have recently lost their source of income.
We feel that the program we have outlined can be put into effect but we must have a full scale war on unemployment. This is the only answer to the problem. It may very well be that this winter we shall have less unemployment than we had last winter and I certainly hope that is the case. The Canadian economy may be dragged up by world economic conditions and particularly by the United States economy, but this will not mean the end of the problem. I hope this government will seize the challenge that confronts it to come to grips with the problem of un-

Supply-Labour
employment by introducing long term measures that will ensure that we will never have in Canada again the levels of unemployment we had last winter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened carefully today to most of the speeches made on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Labour and I must say nearly all were constructive speeches. I thought particularly constructive the speech made by my colleague the hon. member for Essex East with which the minister did not disagree too much, I think, although he did take issue with some of the statistics submitted to him by the hon. member.
The hon. member for Essex East has been our spokesman on this subject for a number of years now. Not only did he give the position of the opposition and of the party but he also spoke with the same authority on this subject as he does on many other subjects.
I should like also to refer particularly to the contribution made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont who dealt I believe more particularly with the Quebec aspect of the situation, although he did speak in general terms as well.
I should like to commend the hon. member for Leeds who, I think all hon. members will agree, is making a serious and substantial impact upon the house by the manner in which he prepares himself for these debates.
The hon. member for Peterborough has just completed a constructive speech. With .many of the things he said I, and I am sure those who sit on this side of the house, [DOT]agree. I was pleased to see him put on the Tecord some of the things that his party would be prepared to do in case of an emergency, having particular reference to the situation in which we find ourselves today. Many of those things were advocated by the Liberal party quite some time ago.
The minister made a long speech. I am glad the committee permitted him to speak at length so that he could put on the record the whole program, as he wished to, of the government in reference to the unemployment situation.
Just some of it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I listened to him carefully and I believe in an impartial way. Judging by the glowing statement he made on behalf of the government, suggesting all that had been done by the government, I would have thought he would have come to the conclusion that something substantial, something consequential, had materialized from what had been done. But that was not the case. If you look at the cold facts of the matter you will find that the situation in Canada in the

month of August was still twice as bad as it was when the present government took office in 1957. If you look at the figures of
323,000	in August 1961, and compare them with the situation in 1957 when 162,000 were unemployed when we left office, notwithstanding the glowing picture painted by the minister, you can draw your own conclusions as to the effect of the program which has been put into operation.
Notwithstanding the rosy picture painted by the minister of the program adopted by the government in many fields there is still one cold fact which no one in this committee can contradict, and it is this. When we left office the unemployment insurance fund was close to $1 billion. Today it is down to $100 million or less. These are cold facts and they give some idea to the committee and the country how it was depleted and of what is happening now.
The minister read from a paragraph of the report of the special committee of the Senate on manpower and employment. I cannot understand why he did not read the whole of the paragraph. At page 21 the minister read these words:
With the wisdom of hindsight one can see in the statistical record evidence of weakness emerging gradually over a period of many years.
He stopped there. I should like to go on. Here is what the report said:
In a sense, though, the 1957-58 recession was a major turning point. The recovery from this recession was relatively moderate and conspicuously short-lived. Widely held expectations about the increase in national output soon turned out to be over-optimistic, and the economy proved incapable of providing the number of new jobs necessary simultaneously to absorb the increases in the labour force and to reduce unemployment to pre-recession levels. The volume of immigration had declined sharply from its 1957 peak and the rate of family formation had fallen off. Overcapacity had developed in many parts of the economy and this situation, which persisted throughout the period of recovery, had a serious effect on investment expenditures. Early in 1960 the economy entered another recession without ever having recovered fully from the preceding one.
From this report on manpower and employment it will appear very clearly that a serious situation began following the 1957 recession. The minister took the figures for the month of August and he was very happy with the result. Let me tell him at once that I, too and we on this side of the house as well, are happy to see a betterment of the situation; notwithstanding the betterment of the situation there are a number of facts which were pointed out by the hon. member for Essex East which I will not, nor do I feel I should, repeat. One of those facts is that there are still 323,000 unemployed in this country. This is a serious matter. Whether it be 5 per

cent of the labour force or 4.3 per cent, it is still a serious matter and the country will want to know what is the position of the government with reference to it. It has been said by the minister that this is a decrease of
31,000	in the month of August as compared with the month of July. That is good. I am pleased; we are happy with that; but in the other sentence in the labour force statistics issued by the Department of Labour the following appears:
The labour force decreased by 39,000, which is more than usual for this period.
This is a sentence which should be read in conjunction with the other statement.
1 do not want to deal at length with any particular part of Canada but I would be remiss if in passing I did not make some reference to the province of Quebec. The minister said very little about it. The unemployment situation in that province in August was 6.3 per cent of the labour force compared with 6.2 per cent a year earlier. In fact, the situation there is worse than it is in any other part of Canada save the maritimes. We have this situation, sir, notwithstanding the fact that the present administration in Quebec-and I do not want to get into a political argument; these are facts which I believe are accurate-has accepted contributions from the federal government with reference to unemployment assistance, which it did not do in previous years. It contributes 40 per cent to the winter works program as compared with absolutely nothing by the administration prior to the present one coming into office in Quebec.
Why not?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
You will have to ask your friends to answer that question.
As I say, we have the situation notwithstanding the fact that the Lesage government have accepted contributions under the Trans-Canada Highway Act, which unquestionably helped the unemployment situation in that province and notwithstanding the fact that government has accepted contributions with reference to access roads to forests and other natural resources areas. The fact is that prior to the advent of the new administration in the province of Quebec only 174 municipalities in that province had applied for and obtained the benefits of the winter works program- these figures are from returns to the house -compared with 1,286 projects under the present Quebec administration as reported on December 14, 1960, and almost 2,000 as of this date. I conclude this part of my remarks by making the statement that the government certainly cannot complain about the co-operation it is receiving in the field of employment and with respect to its so-called
Supply-Labour
program to relieve unemployment so far as the province of Quebec is concerned. Yet notwithstanding the government's program and notwithstanding the contribution by the province, 6.3 per cent of the labour force in the province of Quebec were still out of work in the month of August.
Since the new Liberal regime.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I say that is a serious matter and it is serious because in my opinion the government is not doing nearly enough in that area. The minister has referred to certain projects in the province of Quebec. He has referred to the Champlain bridge which was approved by the former administration. He has referred to the Mattagami railway line which was approved by the house, of course, and which I hope is helping to relieve the situation in that area of the province. Those are the only two projects in the province of Quebec to which he referred. I suggest to him that not nearly enough public projects have been instituted by the government of Canada in that province.
The minister dealt at great length with the program of the government and he put on the record a long list of things which had been done by the government to meet the unemployment situation. But all of the things he put on the record had to do with one aspect of unemployment only, unemployment in the construction field. He suggested absolutely nothing to deal with cyclical unemployment or structural unemployment. He did refer to assistance to depressed areas, about which I will have more to say in a moment. I say to him and to those who sit behind him that 75 per cent-I was going to say 90 per cent but perhaps I would be mistaken-are projects which, if they are of assistance, are of assistance only in one sector of the economy, namely, in the field of building and the allied trades.
There are other areas of the economy which are suffering and for which little is being done. The minister has said nothing about emigration. He did put on record a statement by Mr. Meyer of the Gazette toward the end of his speech but there are other aspects of this matter which I think also deserve to be put on the record. I should like to refer to a newsletter prepared by the department of economic development of the Canadian chamber of commerce, and I quote from the last page thereof:
Stuart Armour, economic adviser, the Steel Company of Canada Limited, speaking to the annual meeting of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, commented: "Can it be that we are attempting to solve our unemployment problem by losing population? Let us hope not, for in 1957, when we

Supply-Labour
had the second highest net migration in the past decade we had a very much higher level of business activity than we are now experiencing".
A little farther on in the letter is this paragraph:
Of particular concern in this connection is the steady flow of emigrants to the United States. In the 12 months ending June 30, 1960, there were 46,668 immigrants to the United States whose country of last permanent residence was Canada. Of this number, 30,132 were born in this country.
Because it is of tremendous importance I repeat that last statement.
Of this number, 30,132 were born in this country. During this period, Canada lost to the United States more than 5,700 professional, technical and kindred workers including professors and instructors, draftsmen, engineers, physicians and surgeons, teachers, technicians, and 1,372 badly needed professional nurses. We lost more than 1,100 managers, officials and proprietors and more than 4,500 craftsmen, foremen and kindred workers, including brick-masons, stonemasons, carpenters, machinists, mechanics, plumbers, plasterers and toolmakers.
I could go on. The decrease in the number of unemployed amounted to 31,000 in the month of August but, as this newsletter indicates, 46,668 persons, of whom 30,132 were born in Canada, emigrated to the United States in the period mentioned. The question arises in our minds at once: Are we to understand that we have to solve our unemployment problem by emigration to the United States?
In one month?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It does not matter whether it is in one month or in 12 months. I am dealing with the 12-month figure, and it is a serious matter that over 46,000 people should have gone to the United States, 30,000 of whom were born in this country. I pose the question because it is one of serious importance for all of us.
The minister dealt with the encouragement the government has given to depressed areas. Perhaps I am not using the right term. I believe another expression has been used by the minister from time to time but I will use "depressed area" for lack of a better phrase. The minister made a great deal of the applications that had been received which he said represented a value of approximately $85 million. So far so good, but how many of those applications have been approved by the government? I think the house has a right to know that. As hon. members know, the purpose of assistance by way of double depreciation is double-barrelled, as the minister has stated. First, it is to come to the assistance of an industry which might develop a new product anywhere in Canada. Double depreciation will be granted to such an industry. Second, if an industry decides to establish itself in an

area so designated by the government it will receive double depreciation for one year.
I want to know how many applications for double depreciation have been accepted by the government and, second, I want to know how many men have been put to work as a result of this program. I doubt very much whether one man has been put to work by virtue of the action taken by the government in this field. The next question is, what areas of Canada have been declared by the government to be depressed areas? The minister stated that the municipal authorities were interested in this program, that by early September 49 applications had been made and eight local areas and 11 specific locations had been designated. We said at the time that this was not the way to do it, that is the method whereby the municipalities should make application to one or the other of the departments of government. We said the government should itself take the initiative because it would know from what information it had, be it in labour, be it in trade and commerce, be it in public works or in finance or any other department, which areas were the depressed areas. I say with respect, of course, that when the minister dealt with that part of his program, in so far as meeting the unemployment situation was concerned in my opinion that was the weakest part of his contribution to this debate.
Even under the best of conditions of full employment at the national level, certain sectors of the Canadian economy have experienced stagnation. There is no doubt about that, it is admitted by all of us. This is due, in part, to the geographical dispersion of industries and the tendency towards regional concentration of single industries. When there are any shifts in consumer preference, changes in technology, depletion of resources or a resurgence of world competition, the local industry's market position is constricted, but the severest impact is on the locality that is totally dependent upon the industry. The disappearance of such an industry, although it leaves a vacuum gives no assurance that the vacuum will be filled by a new industry.
There are certain economic factors which contribute to labour immobility, so there is no outflow of workers to bring the supply and demand of labour into equilibrium. Under conditions of less than full employment or severe unemployment such as existed in Canada since 1957, the problems of the distressed areas are greatly aggravated. As the house knows, the average unemployment for the year 1958 was 7.1 per cent; 1959, 6 per cent and 1960, 7 per cent. The Canadian government is pledged to a national goal of

lull employment. The white paper on unemployment which was tabled in this house many years ago by the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe stated unequivocally that full employment was the major goal of government policy. Here was a policy to deal with the post-war transitional period laid down clearly. There were 11 points which dealt with the situation, not as we found it then, but as we anticipated it might be. First, the employment problem was dealt with; next, the sources of employment and income were described; then export trade was dealt with, private investment in Canada, consumption, public investment, scientific and industrial research, placement and training of workers, wartime controls, government financing, the beginning of the transition. Anyone reading this short pamphlet can come to no other conclusion but that here was a program which had been thought out; here was a program that had been brought about by the meeting of many of the best minds in our country. It was this program that helped Canada go through the post-war period from 1945 to 1957 in a manner which resulted in no more than three per cent on the average of the labour force being out of work at any time, and 3 per cent was considered by economists as full employment.
That is false.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My friend behind me says that is false. I have put on the record on many occasions the statistics and they are there for whoever wants to see them.
In order to accomplish full employment, these regional pockets to which I have been referring of chronic unemployment must be eliminated. They must be eradicated since they have reached such proportions as to become an effective brake on the economic capacity of the nation to attain and sustain an adequate rate of growth. If any further justification is needed for an all-out federal attack on the problem of distressed areas, one has only to refer to the report of the Senate committee on manpower and employment. At this point, I should like to quote from page 69, as follows:
This is not to suggest that technological change and the provision of cheaper goods by foreign suppliers are without benefit. Their benefits are obvious. Nevertheless, it must be recognized that they sometimes create serious problems for particular industries and, in so far as these industries are geographically concentrated rather than spread uniformly across the country, the problems may manifest themselves in particular areas. In other words, while the benefits of technological advance and cheaper imports may be widely distributed the unfavourable effects may be geographically confined.
This quotation substantiates the statement which I have just made. There are, as the
90205-6-547
Supply-Labour
minister knows, specific distressed areas in the Canadian economy that endure, at the present time, one and a half to two times the national average in amount of unemployment. The duration of the unemployment is just as important as the rate. Long term unemployment, that is unemployment over 15 weeks during the year is prevalent in these areas. A long period of unsuccessful job seeking usually represents a real crisis in the personal life of the individual and an irrecoverable loss both to the individual and to the economy of his productive capacity which goes unused during this time. An excess of supply over demand in labour for long periods of time in distressed areas, coupled with the immobility of the labour supply, due to such things as home ownership or lack of information on alternative job opportunities outside of the region leads to a lack of hope and despair on the part of the individual involved. The loss of income on the personal level results in communities being unable to provide essential services. This deficiency in essential services, when coupled with problems of providing welfare, constitutes an impossible financial burden on the stricken community.
How is this problem being met? The minister has indicated in his earlier remarks what the government has done. But I say to him with respect that that part of his program is inadequate to meet the situation as we find it today in the depressed areas across Canada. Here, I should like to quote what Professor Stanislaw Judek of the University of Ottawa had to say in his submission to the Senate committee on manpower, and which was in a large part adopted. He said:
The attempt to ease unemployment on a seasonal
basis-
I ask the committee to listen to this carefully.
-through an inadequate winter works program and on an industry basis, mainly through housing and other construction projects, is not sufficient in the long run because it does not recognize the condition of persistent local unemployment. Other more acceptable alternatives and long term measures must be devised to deal with structural unemployment and localized unemployment.
Here is a person who has given a great deal of thought to this aspect of unemployment and these are his views.
What is needed is a systematic study of our economic regions which will form the basis for the national employment policy. To overcome this problem, the federal government must provide technical aid for regional areas and supplement a region-wide plan by means of grants and low interest loans, and by means of tax incentives to promote the location of industries in distressed areas. What

Supply-Labour
we need to do is to return to the philosophy of the white paper on employment, as submitted to the house in 1945, which states, and I quote:
-that the dominion (government) will undertake its own deferred projects in those localities in which decline of war contracts or other circumstances have made available labour which can be included on such projects and for which the localities give promise of permanent employment.
It was this philosophy that enabled Canadians to demobilize with a minimum of dislocation and to generate a rate of growth from 1945 to 1957, which was the envy of every country in the world. That is not the condition in Canada today. I have already put on the record some of the statements made by persons in the common market countries. When they were told what to do by members of this government they replied, "You should be minding your own business and not telling us what to do, because your own economic situation is in a bad way".
Such a national employment policy as that which I have been attempting to lead up to would, of course, necessitate co-ordination. It would necessitate co-ordinated government activity at all levels. It should have as its first goal the upgrading of the skills of the unemployed in distressed areas so that they will be able to find alternative employment; second, to increase the number of jobs available in the distressed areas; third, to slow down or prevent the development of new areas of chronic unemployment.
I should like to put on the record now the steps which we on this side of the chamber or a Liberal administration would look to in order to eradicate unemployment in distressed areas.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman proceeds, I must advise the committee that his time has expired.
Go on.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent to allowing the hon. gentleman to continue?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, The steps to which I refer are as follows:
1.	Establishment of a national advisory board on economic development, automation and employment, that would work in coordination with local development agencies, co-ordinating their efforts and providing technical assistance at the local level.
2.	Detailed economic regional development plans based on adequate research for each distressed area.

3.	Tax exemptions to encourage enterprise to locate in distressed areas.
4.	Accelerated depreciation over the whole term of investment.
5.	Special treatment of retained earnings that are specially needed in distressed areas.
6.	Massive vocational and retraining programs to prepare people for jobs in the regional or national labour market, worked out in conjunction with provincial authorities so as not to infringe on provincial rights.
7.	Supplementary unemployment benefits paid to those willing to undergo instructive training.
8.	Federal assistance in the preparation of local development programs. Contributions towards urban renewal both for labour and capital costs to the end of restoring lands to effective commercial and industrial use in distressed areas.
9.	Expansion of the terms of reference of the industrial development bank so as to supplement the regions' financial capacity, to seek effective action against unemployment.
10.	Co-ordinate monetary and fiscal policy in order to promote the proper atmosphere for general growth in the economy, thus relieving the local incidence of unemployment and providing alternative sources of employment outside the region for those willing and able to move out of surplus labour areas.
The committee has been good enough to give its consent to allowing me extra time and I am not going to abuse the privilege. However, before I take my seat, I wish to say a word about some of the things to which the minister referred, but I shall do it briefly.
The minister referred at some length to the public works projects that were being put into effect by this government. He referred to the Columbia river project. The committee, of course, knows that no one has been employed because of this project, although the treaty between Canada and the United States was signed many months ago; and it was signed notwithstanding the fact that no assurance had been obtained from the provincial government involved, namely the government of British Columbia, that it would be willing to go along with the project.
The minister referred to the Pine Point railway. We have just this morning approved this project in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. We have the word of the minister that the survey will not be completed until the end of the year. Hence there is certainly no ground for making the

statement that benefits will flow from this project at least before it gets started, and I doubt whether that will be prior to 1962.
Then the minister referred to the Beech-wood project. This project was finished before the loan was given. How could it provide any jobs? I have dealt with three of the five projects to which the minister referred.
Then the minister had a great deal to say about the national productivity council. However, he did not say much about what the chairman of the national productivity council was saying. Does the government and the minister approve the statements and speeches made by Mr. De Young? Can the minister state whether or not be he approves of the pronouncements that have been made by the Mr. De Young? A moment ago he said the government had no control over the productivity council. However, the government also had no control over the Bank of Canada. The government also did not like the speeches made by the then governor of the Bank of Canada. Are we again in a position similar to that in which we were with reference to the government going one way with its economic policy and the Minister of Finance being dissatisfied with the other arm of government the Bank of Canada? Is that the position with reference to the minister and the national productivity council? I wish he had said more about that matter.
Then he spoke at some length about the winter works program. I put on the record a statement made by a professor from the University of Ottawa before the manpower committee of the Senate. The minister himself referred to it and I need not repeat what he said. As to the winter works program, however, let it not be forgotten by the committee that, although the government calls it its program, only one third of the funds are provided by the federal government. The rest of the funds come either from the municipalities or the provincial governments. Notwithstanding that fact, the figures I have been given are that this employed about 85,000 people, many of whom would have been put to work under any circumstances.
The minister went far afield of his department in dealing with other extraneous conditions and circumstances that have helped the position of employment in Canada. For instance, he told us about the anti-dumping legislation. How could the anti-dumping legislation enter into the matter, when it has never been used by the government, unless I am mistaken, except perhaps once or twice. Notwithstanding the fact that we protested against this legislation and were condemned for protesting against it, the very reasons we 90205-6-547J
Supply-Labour
put forward for not passing it are some of the reasons the government is now using for not putting it into effect.
I have dealt with the national productivity council as briefly as I could. The minister spoke about trade. I do not want to get into an argument about what happened at Accra. I will keep away from that matter as there will be an opportunity to deal with it later.
I do not know about that. The Minister of Finance is not coming back until Christmas.
He is having a second honeymoon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
However, let it not be forgotten that this government had the opportunity to assist in the promotion of jobs by accepting the free trade offer from the United Kingdom. However, it turned its back on that offer. To use an expression which the Minister of Finance likes to use in the house from time to time, the government ran away from this free trade offer just as fast as its legs could carry it. There is no doubt about that. Now the government is critical of the United Kingdom because it is about to make application to join the common market. I do not intend to talk about the tendency of this government toward protection, a tendency which certainly does not help employment. Proof of that can be found in the period of time which elapsed from 1930 to 1935. We do not want to go back to those conditions when we "blasted our country into the markets of the world". When we adopt that kind of language rather than attempt to make a deal with the tremendous potential market of the E.C.M. containing some 220 million people, we are certainly not acting in our best interests. I think the method which seems to have been adopted by the ministers, as well as by the government up till now does not seem to be one conducive to the promotion or expansion of jobs, but rather to the restriction of jobs.
All I need to say in conclusion is that I have attempted to deal with a specific aspect of this question, namely unemployment in distressed areas. I do not think-and I say this again to the minister with respect-that he has dealt effectively with this problem. I have tried also to put on record in Hansard some thoughts which I believe may be helpful. If we were to follow those suggestions I am hopeful that in the distressed areas-and there are far more of them in Canada than the minister would seem to indicate-a much larger dent in unemployment in Canada would be effected than is being made at the present time.

I believe nearly every member of this committee understands that I represent an urban constituency in the east of the city of Vancouver. I think I am safe in saying that almost 100 per cent of my riding is a working class residential area. It is therefore understandable that in this constituency of Vancouver East we have had a very serious problem arising from unemployment and it would be almost axiomatic that in rising to speak on this, the first item, of the estimates of the Minister of Labour, I should have an emphatic speech to make on unemployment, its cause and its cure. It is not my intention to do that. I may be criticized for this, but I do not believe in political expediency or in useless repetition. I believe that since the discussion opened on this item just about everything that could be said has been said with regard to the seriousness of unemployment, its causes and the means by which it might be cured. So why should I take up the time of this committee by repetition? I do not intend to do so.
My purpose in rising to speak on this item is to raise one question with regard to which I should like to have an answer from the Minister of Labour. The question is this: what attitude does the minister take toward the I.L.O.? The international labour organization is a body which in my view has been ignored by this government for far too long, as it has been by previous governments. As I am sure you know, Mr. Chairman, the international labour organization is the oldest of the major specialized agencies which function today as part of the United Nations family. I am sure that many of us forget that the organization came into being as far back as April, 1919, under the terms of the Treaty of Versailles. It was, and still is, a tripartite international agency. Its policy-a wonderful one-has been accepted, namely that there should be government, employer and worker representation from all parts of the world.
According to the last report in June of this year there were 100 nations in the organization. I do not think it is generally recognized that Canada was a founding member in April of 1919. Here we have on an international basis an organization whose policy and principles could with advantage be further advanced in the domestic field in Canada. I should like to hear from the minister his views on the international aspect of Canada's representation on the I.L.O. I shall put it this way: the international labour organization promotes the voluntary co-operation of industrial nations in an effort to improve labour conditions and to raise living standards. I think that the instrument through which the I.L.O. is making the greatest contribution to the welfare of the workers and

the farmers of the world is through what is known as the international labour code. This code is based on what are termed conventions, and since the first meeting of the I.L.O. in 1919,	115 conventions have been passed.
Canada, with government, industry and workers represented, has taken part in the passing in Geneva of those 115 conventions.
What is the purpose behind the I.L.O.? Hon. members will find it in the constitution of the organization. As stated in that constitution, the I.L.O. was founded on the fundamental tenet that universal and lasting peace could best be established only if it were based on social justice. I did not know until recently that the I.L.O. had a motto. Its motto is: Poverty anywhere is a danger to prosperity everywhere. Canada was a founding member of the international labour organization in 1919. I am informed that 115 conventions have been passed by the I.L.O. in Geneva since that date with Canada supporting most of them. However, out of that number Canada has ratified only 19, most of which deal with the welfare of seamen, their standards of food, etc. Canada's record is one of the poorest of all the states and nations that make up the I.L.O. I shall place on the record figures relating to the number of conventions ratified by other countries in order that hon. members of the committee may appreciate what a rotten record Canada has:
No. of Conventions Ratified since
Country	1919
Belgium	 60
Italy	 59
United Kingdom	 58
Uruguay	 57
Norway	 52
New Zealand	 41
Sweden	  38
Canada	 19
This is an important matter. I feel that we are entitled to ask the Minister of Labour what the position of the government is with respect to the I.L.O.
I received last week from the I.L.O. a chart dated June 1, 1961 outlining all the conventions adopted by the I.L.O. since 1919. In the four years during which the present minister has held office Canada ratified only one convention, No. 105. To what did it refer? The abolition of forced labour.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Is the hon. member against that?

Of course we support the ratification of this convention. We have in Canada what I wish to describe for the purposes of these remarks as a constitutional, democratic, parliamentary federalism. Strict lines of demarcation are drawn between the

jurisdiction of the federal and provincial governments and perhaps the minister will take refuge in that argument. However, 1 emphasize that it is a damnable disgrace that no action has been taken to improve Canada's record with respect to the ratification of I.L.O. conventions. We should be ashamed of our record; but, taking pride in the fact that we were a founding member in 1919, action should be taken to ratify, in the respective jurisdictions, the I.L.O. conventions which are of a constructive nature.
I do not think this matter has been raised in the chamber before and so, because the points I would have made concerning unemployment were all covered I chose not to repeat them but to bring this matter to the attention of the committee. I urge the minister and the government to take action to improve Canada's record with respect to the ratification of I.L.O. conventions so that if Canada is not at the top of the list it will at least be close to the top in terms of the number of conventions ratified.

I believe that the hon. member for Vancouver East has raised a point which interests not only labour unions in this country, but also management, as well as every Canadian and especially all members of this house.
If some of the unemployed have read the speech of my hon. colleague from St. Mary (Mr. Valade), they must have derived much comfort from learning that they belong to the category of frictional, cyclic, seasonal or finally technical unemployment. It must be for them a cause of great satisfaction to know to what class of unemployed they belong.
As recorded on page 8628 of the Hansard of September 20, the hon. member for St. Mary had this to say while speaking about the responsibility for unemployment:
In this respect, I should like to quote the statement made by the ephemeral leader, Hon. Jean Lesage, head of the Liberal party in Quebec.
In the language I tried hard to learn, to quote someone means to repeat literally and faithfully what that person said. The hon. member for St. Mary however did give but a paraphrase of what the Hon. Mr. Lesage had said in the province, and if this is not true, I want the hon. member to call me to order.
The Hon. Mr. Lesage never stated that unemployment was exclusively a provincial

responsibility as far as Quebec is concerned. He said that the province of Quebec had also to assume some responsibility for the unemployment problem, since it concerns the citizens of that province.
I think that by such a statement, the leader of the province, proved not only realistic but also courageous, since he repeated it after he had been elected to the position he now holds.
If the hon. member for St. Mary has reported with as much accuracy the speech delivered by Mr. Hamel on television, I think it is not necessary to carry on a controversy with him on that matter.
However, all I should like to add is that the government of the province of Quebec has already started taking action in that field.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier), on the other hand, has mentioned some action that has been taken since the election of the Liberal government in the province of Quebec.
In the field of winter works only, I think, the government has done a lot and the province of Quebec comes first as far as federal government proposals are concerned. Incidentally, I would be dishonest if I failed to recognize that the winter works program initiated by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) means something to this country in the matter of employment. But, as my colleagues who spoke before me said, the program is not adequate and too many people still cannot earn a living in this country.
The number of Quebec municipalities which submitted projects to the federal government in 1958-59 was 67; for the 1959-60 fiscal year, 93; for the 1960-61 fiscal year, 535.
The projects approved by the federal administration in 1958-59 numbered 289; in the fiscal year 1959-60, 336 and in 1960-61, 2,027, out of a total of 7,095 for the ten provinces.
The total expenditures involved by the various projects submitted by the provinces, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, as well as by the Indian reservations, amounted to $289,911,087, in the fiscal year 1960-61. The province of Quebec alone submitted projects amounting to approximately $125,732,715. I think that the province of Quebec has tried to do something, and that it has really taken concrete steps to alleviate the unemployment problem, in the quickest way possible; but immediate steps are not the only thing required to alleviate the unemployment problem. Since 1957, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and some others of my colleagues have been submitting

Supply-Labour
to the house all kinds of projects designed to provide a long term solution to the unemployment problem.
I am not interested in knowing who is responsible for unemployment. I am interested in the fate of those who are jobless and want to work.
Whenever we make a suggestion implying long term legislation to the government, we are accused of never submitting anything realistic which might immediately relieve unemployment.
To quote only one instance, in Quebec-and the federal administration recently took similar action-we set up, as I said, an economic guidance council for the province. One of the principal aims of the council is to decentralize industries and to see to it that some are established in those communities which suffer more particularly from the blight of unemployment.
A start was also made on plans to set up a steel industry in Quebec. Indeed, an investment fund of $1 hundred million will be available to industrialists who want to establish such an industry in the province.
At this time, the prime minister of the province of Quebec is in Europe, where he very actively is trying to obtain capital with a view to setting up that industry.
Other suggestions were made by my colleagues and others, and I shall not linger on the subject.
Yet, before sitting down again, I want to reiterate a suggestion which I have frequently made in this house. I am sure that it has much merit, as it was made by the Prime Minister of my country (Mr. Diefenbaker), when he addressed the citizens of Canada in 1957. Indeed, in a talk at the Montreal chamber of commerce, on February 19, 1957, he said:
(Text):
Every encouragement must be given to the processing of domestic raw materials in Canada to a much greater degree than prevails, in order that our resources may he utilized to the maximum advantage of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I agree that the establishment of industries like those is not possible overnight, but those statements were made more than four years ago by the Prime Minister and he then promised the nation that he would do something in that field.
