Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak for a few minutes about one aspect of conditions in Newfoundland which has a direct bearing on the minister's department. I refer to the almost complete failure of the codfishery in many parts of Newfoundland and Labrador during the past season. As the minister is very likely aware, in southern Labrador and the northeast coast of Newfoundland and other parts as well-I speak particularly of my own riding which I know best-the codfishery was almost a complete failure.
Last year the fishery was very poor but this year it was even worse and many fishermen will not have sufficient fish this year to qualify for fishermen's unemployment insurance. This second bad season has caused and is causing acute need in many communities. I wish the minister would consider the possibility of including some of these small fishing communities in his winter works program. I have in mind in particular a community stage building program similar to the one now about to be completed. I think the last community stage in the present program is being built at the present time.
I might add that such a program stands on its own merits as a worth-while contribution toward increasing the efficiency of the fishing industry but it would be doubly important if a community stage building program could be considered at this time in connection with the need for work. This in fact would mean a good program being put to an even better use.
I would ask the minister to consider immediately the advisability of another community stage program to be initiated as soon as possible so that the fishermen in these communities where community stages might be built will have the opportunity of working during the winter to procure the necessary materials. As you know, winter work in Newfoundland, particularly in the northern areas, means late fall or early spring work, but materials for community stages could be procured during the winter.
There is one other point I should like to mention, the desirability of making Newfoundland a separate region in so far as the administration of unemployment insurance is concerned. This matter has been mentioned before. When disputed claims have to be referred to Moncton it means further delay.

Supply-Labour
I should like to suggest that Newfoundland be made a separate region and that it should not be considered as merely a part of the larger Atlantic region. I should also like to suggest that Gander might be a central place from which such a region could be administered.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to speak in this debate. I think those who have been in the house since I have been a member know that I do not rise on many occasions. I do not seek newspaper headlines or rise merely to repeat many of the things that have already been said in a debate. I have listened carefully to the debate on these estimates and I should like to say that the interest shown by hon. members in this problem is no greater than my own. Any individual who tries to wear a particularly bright and shining halo around his head in expressing his concern about these matters is only trying to fool the public and seek publicity.
I think all members who have spoken in this debate have done so because of their serious concern and genuine interest. However, there were many inaccuracies in some of the speeches that were made and I can see only one reason for the continued repetition of these inaccuracies, namely, that there are certain members in the house whose interest in their political future is such that on every occasion they rise to speak they have to conduct a baby election campaign on a provincial or federal basis. I think that those who do these things are much less effective in their presentations to the house. Much has been said at times about interruptions but when some hon. members do these things I suggest that they invite interruptions. I am not given to interruption. I exploded once during the speech of the hon. member for Peterborough and I would apologize to him if I disrupted the tenor of his thought. I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members that I am credited with a couple of interruptions yesterday in this debate. They were not mine. I did not make them and I hope that the member who did will take the opportunity tomorrow to have them credited to himself.
I want to commend the Minister of Labour upon the realistic, proper and responsible manner in which he placed before the committee a factual report of the government program, after the many needles that had been thrust at him in a very polished manner. He gave us a statement of the results and the hopes for the future. He outlined these in a fashion that I think everyone should understand and I want to commend him for it. This was not done in a partisan manner and I believe hon. members of the house who know

the minister, know his background and know his interest in this problem, know that his attitude is one of genuine concern and his method is that of co-operation.
The hon. member for Leeds made what I thought was, in many respects, an interesting speech. However, he made some remarks which I am afraid indicate that he has already become infected by the environment of these former cabinet ministers who will not accept the verdict of the Canadian people and realize that the policies they had, for which they claim such glory and greatness, were rejected by these people. The arguments placed before the committee by the hon. member for Leeds were less effective because of this fact.
The hon. member for Trinity raised a matter which bothers me a good deal. It lies on my heart in a heavy manner. I refer to the decision taken by the government, because of the world situation, to recruit for the army and the militia. These steps were taken with only one thought in mind, to provide for the survival of our way of life, our country and our people. The innuendo that this step was taken for the purpose of lessening the impact of unemployment this winter and so that the true unemployment picture would be covered up, is one for which I believe the hon. member should apologize. This suggestion was echoed by the hon. member for Leeds in his speech. I took down his words, and here is what he said: The government is expanding our army, and thank God; that will reduce unemployment. I just cannot understand any responsible citizen of this country, for any purpose whatever suggesting that the government took this step in order to cover up the true unemployment picture. I do not believe the Canadian public will think very much of hon. members who make such suggestions.
I have heard a great deal about the great 22 years of Liberalism and the greatness of those men, some of whom are sitting here now. The only happy warrior amongst them is the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate. He is the only one sitting in this house who has said, "The people of Canada kicked us out and I will accept their verdict. I am an opposition man now, but I will be getting back over there some day." There are many hon. members who are unable to make a constructive speech. They introduce extraneous matters, such as provincial elections.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Your members are experts at bringing in provincial matters.

Some of our members do that perhaps, but I wish they would not follow

the example of some of your members as often as they do. However, I do not intend to do so.
It would seem from the criticism that has been offered in the speeches made since the minister spoke that some members cannot appreciate the information he gave in a factual manner because hon. members have continued to use their narrow arguments purely for the benefit of their political parties.
We will be back in soon.

I say to the committee that as long as there is one person in this country who is unemployed and who really wants to work, I am concerned. I, too, would say to the government your measures have not done enough. I have had some very good experiences in this connection because I have lived in the one community for over 30 years. On occasion I have been in the position that caused people to come to me. I can recall one boy who came to me on many occasions seeking work. I checked his background, checked his employment picture and tried to help him. I tried to find out what his own efforts had been to find work. On the last occassion I saw him he had another young fellow with him. He introduced me to this young fellow, who was his cousin. I said, where are you from, and ascertained he came from a farm 120 miles from Regina. The boy with whom I had been dealing had been out of work for six months, but his cousin from the farm came into town and found a job within four days. The government cannot do everything. People who try to help cannot do everything. There must be within the individual a real desire and a real effort to find work.
The hon. member can correct me if I am wrong, but I think it was the hon. member for Laurier who said that at no time before 1957 had the unemployment average in Canada been greater than 3 per cent. On page 59 of the French version of the Senate committee report on manpower I notice that in 1950 it was 3.6 per cent; in 1954, 4.6 per cent and in 1955, 4.4 per cent. Those are figures taken from this report. I wanted to make this correction because this is one of those inaccuracies which has been repeated and repeated and I felt I must correct it.
However, I do not believe it has much to do with the problem. We know we have unemployment today. We all want to solve the problem. I want to commend the government for the action they have taken. I believe that towards the end of the remarks of the
Supply-Labour
hon. member for Peterborough, if I understood him correctly, he said that the government planned in the long term. I agree with that. I say to him that some of the measures the government has adopted are long term measures. We heard a remark to the effect that as soon as we removed the tax on automobiles, the Ontario Conservative government imposed a 3 per cent tax. Well, I have lived under your socialist policies, I have lived under your great authoritarian planning and I recall that over 20 years ago the Liberals imposed a sales tax. Your party, who are so honest and keep all their promises, said they would remove this iniquitous tax completely. They took office, but they did not take any action. Then, another election came along and they reduced the tax by 1 per cent, saying that as soon as other sources of revenue were available they would abolish it.
The year before this government took office the province had an income from federal sources, grants and so on of $34 million. Last year this income amounted to some $76 million, but we have not had any reduction in taxation, not a nickel. Before they got the 50-50 deal for hospitalization-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I take
advantage of the pause on the part of the hon. member in order to remind him that we are on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Labour. He seems to be straying a little bit away from that topic.

Many of the other members who preceded me in speaking also strayed from the topic. I am only answering, in the only way in which I can do so, some of the arguments they advanced. I say that we have had over 20 years of socialist rule in Saskatchewan. Those people or that little group of them with all the brains in the country, want to sit in a room and tell you, me and everyone else in the country what we should do. They should look at what is happening in Saskatchewan and find out how futile it is. Democratic free people do not want that sort of planning done for them. In a democracy the people want an opportunity to exercise their skill and to get the benefit for so doing and to expand the economy. That sort of planning does not do it.
We are supposed to have had Utopia in Saskatchewan for almost a quarter of a century, or it is getting on to that length of time. It will not reach that stage, however, because the next election will fix the situation. Nevertheless we have the lowest rate of growth in Canada. Our population has never got back to the figure at which it stood when the socialists came into power. Our people are still going to places where they do not have all these great benefits of these fine planners.

Supply-Labour
They find it better to go there. Perhaps at the moment they are not well off but they have opportunity. I do not want to see this thing happen at the federal level as then we would really have stagnation of the economy.
A planned economy.

It has been said that we ran away from the free trade offer at the conference. That reference was made by someone. I do not know whether or not he is a free trader. When he is out west he is quite a free trader and at times I have had occasion to hear him expound his views. But when he is down east and when he is in this House of Commons and is trying to make sure that he comes back here again, it seems to me that he is anything but a free trader inasmuch as he would bar from coming into Canada every foreign automobile that some of our people like to buy and to drive, thereby providing money so that we can have twoway trade.
I heard remarks made about this government's seeking to have more material processed in Canada; I refer to raw material. Yet every time they take some action that would assist in the matter, they are accused of having a high tariff policy.
I think I have said enough. I just say, in closing, that I have not had to speak in the house in order to put my views before a government whose concern is second to none- it is certainly as great as that of any group in this House of Commons-and whose actions indicate that they work closely together, that the program of each department is concentrated and coagulated in order to gain results-
Coagulated?

The hon. member can pick me up if I use some wrong words. However, I think hon. members know what I mean. I did not prepare a speech and come here with a great deal of material. I am speaking as I feel. When, because he is frustrated and is sitting where he does not want to sit at the moment because of the judgment of the Canadian people, anyone tries to destroy, by insinuations and inaccuracies, the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet, may I say to that person that the next time the people have an opportunity to express themselves by their vote, he will find out that such a policy is futile.
I look forward to the government expanding its projects. I know they are digging fully and completely into these matters and are expanding their projects with a view to reducing this problem. I would not say that I would be complacent, satisfied and happy when the figure reaches 3 per cent, by diligently seeking and looking for improvements, we can

reduce it below that figure. The unemployment problem will never be gone, however because there are people who are not built in such a way that they want to work steadily. There are people who would like to relax at the expense of the taxpayers. We shall always have them. However, the lower we can get the figure of those that are unemployed, the happier we should all be, whether or not it redounds to our benefit politically.

I am sure the committee listened with great interest to the speech of the handsome, well-fed and well groomed member for Regina who has had to live under a C.C.F. government for something over 16 years. From the tenor of his speech I presume it is his valedictory address in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: He is not quite as well fed as is Clarence Fines.

His approach to the problem of unemployment on the estimates under discussion was somewhat different from that which has prevailed in this debate today. I thought it struck a rather depressing note when dealing with a serious question which we should approach in a non partisan spirit although we may differ in our suggestions as to objectives and proposals.
I listened with great interest to the minister's outline of the government's actions to date and its efforts to meet the unemployment situation. However I must say this. While we welcome and support all the efforts that this or any other government has made to meet this serious problem which confronts members of this House of Commons and a great number of Canadians, I think it is quite fair to say that the minister painted a somewhat rosy picture. In the first instance, we all know that the federal government pays only one-third of the cost of the winter works program. Therefore they must not take credit for more than one third of the expenditure in that connection. In the second place, the government shares with provincial governments the cost of a good many other projects. That is all to the good. Then he mentioned the Pine Point railway. We all know that, if the surveys are not now completed, with winter coming on it is not likely that there will be any employment on that railroad, owing to the geographical location of the road, until some time early next summer.
Then I was rather interested to hear him mention the Columbia river project as a possibility of providing employment. May I say this. In my opinion to mention the Columbia river project is to treat a vision as a reality.

However, that procedure has become rather a habit in these later days in this house.
Six o'clock.
I am not criticizing the minister as an individual. I am speaking through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister.
He is a victim.
He is a victim of the system under which we live. He is Minister of Labour in a capitalist society. I speak to him as a member of the working class, expounding their views.
Oh, Oh.
Six o'clock.
It is six o'clock, Mr. Chairman. Some hon. members are rather anxious for me to conclude.
Carried.

In order to facilitate the passage of the estimates I will say on some other item the few things I had intended to say on this one. I do not intend to be long. I do not want to hold up the estimates. However I have one or two gems of wisdom I wish to bring to the minister's attention.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 178 carry?
Carried.

Item agreed to.
179. Economics and research branch including research grants and related expenses, $821,935.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 179 carry?

No. It is six o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7.30 p.m.

I note that in vote 179 there is an increase of $82,008 provided for the economics and research branch this year. I believe there was considerable discussion last year when this item came up. Questions were put to the minister with regard to the kind of reports which are made to him from time to time, estimates for quarter periods ahead or even for 12 month periods ahead, the idea being that as a result of these assessments one might be able to draw some conclusion as to what could be expected in the way of growth of employment or a further increase in unemployment.
Supply-Laoour
We are, naturally, all interested in the unemployment figures as well as in the employment figures. The advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission has indicated that it believes that in the 1961-62 period there will be unemployment comparable to that which we experienced last winter. Of course, this would be unfortunate and it would have serious economic and social consequences. We all hope this will not be the case. But in the light of the vote provided here, the minister ought to be served with these prognostications as to future levels of manpower and employment.
I think the economics and research branch formerly presided over by the distinguished deputy minister ought to be in a position to inform the committee what we may expect for the next ten or 12 months. I should like to know what the anticipations are for the period until the end of December and for the period from January to, let us say, the middle of June. I have a suspicion that the branch devotes much of its activity to manpower studies. If that is the case the minister should be in a position to give some assessment from the information supplied to him as to the probabilities of employment in the immediate future.
We do know that in the Department of Trade and Commerce in other years a confidential and private economic survey was prepared from which the government could draw conclusions in this regard. We also know that the Bank of Canada prepares summaries, half yearly, I think, as well as yearly. It would be interesting to know, particularly in the light of last year's discussion, what the minister has available in this regard. I made the statement yesterday that the practice has been to issue quarterly statements. This was certainly the practice when I was familiar with the department. These statements were, of course, privileged. They were the minister's prerogative and the hon. gentleman may so regard them now. If that is the case, perhaps within those limits, the minister could, nevertheless, give the committee some indication of what he anticipates would be the employment situation in Canada in the next ten or 12 months.

The hon. gentleman answered his own question at the end of what he had to say with respect to the reports. He has had experience as parliamentary assistant to the minister of labour and he must certainly know that these reports are available to the minister. They are compiled by the economics branch from whatever information the branch is able to gather. They make guesses as to what may happen in the immediate future, and only in the immediate

Supply-Labour
future. These reports are, naturally, available to the minister but, as the hon. gentleman himself pointed out, they are confidential. They have remained confidential and are so at the present time.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, you will permit me to say a word about the international labour organization. The hon. member for Vancouver East asked certain questions with respect to the ratification of the conventions which have been adopted by the organization since its inception in 1919. Although that was raised under the first item may I be permitted at this stage to give the information to the hon. member for Vancouver East. I personally look upon the I.L.O. as an important organization. The fact that it has a membership of some 100 countries lends credence to the fact that it is highly regarded by practically all countries in the world.
The Department of Labour has a special section that devotes its time to the functions and activities of the I.L.O. Although it is a matter of regret to me, I personally have not had the opportunity of attending as many of these sessions as I should have liked. My only opportunity was in 1958 at which time I appreciated very much the opportunity to learn of the work of the I.L.O. during my visit. During that short period I observed that the Canadian representatives of workers and employers were treated with great respect. Many of our representatives serve as chairmen of committees and in other responsible positions in the work of the I.L.O. This pleases me very much and I take pride in the fact that the contribution of Canadians is recognized in this way.
Without casting a reflection on the hon. member for Vancouver East may I say in passing that I think he was one who criticized me for being absent from the house at the time of my visit and I have not visited again since then.
I am sorry to interrupt but I challenge the minister to produce from the records a statement attributed to me in which I criticized the minister for being absent on official business.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Read Hansard.
I believe I returned on the evening of the same day the hon. member questioned my whereabouts.
I remember an occasion when the minister was precluded from attending because his estimates were not completed.
Due in part to the efforts of the hon. member for Essex East I was precluded from attending the 1959 session.
Unemployment levels were very high at that time.

I regard the work of the house as being of primary importance, coming before all else. Since its inception the I.L.O. has adopted 115 conventions. I am not too familiar with what happened in the past with respect to the ratification by Canada of these various conventions but since 1957 11 conventions have been adopted by the I.L.O. Conventions Nos. 108, 109, 112, 113 and 114 were adopted in 1958 and 1959. In the main they related to the maritimes and fisheries. Consultations with respect to these five conventions are now being considered by this department and the departments of transport and fisheries with respect to the possibility of ratifying all or some of them. No decision has yet been arrived at and the five conventions are still in process of study.
Only one has been ratified since the minister took office.

In 1958 we ratified a convention adopted in 1957 with respect to the abolition of forced labour. Convention No. 106 having to do with weekly rest in commerce and offices, No. 107 concerning indigenous and tribal populations, No. Ill concerning discrimination and No. 115 relating to radiation protection, lead us into jurisdictional difficulties. Under our federal system we encounter a snag because these conventions relate to fields which partly come under provincial jurisdiction and thus, under our system, the federal government is prevented from ratifying them.
May I ask what steps are being taken to reach an understanding on the matter with the provinces?
This is one area where an attempt could be made to rectify the situation through consultation with the provinces and perhaps we could look into this matter.
Is the department doing so?

I said that we could explore the possibility of achieving some understanding with the provinces in determining whether they would be agreeable to the ratification of these conventions.
Convention No. 110 has to do with the employment of plantation workers and is not applicable in Canada. I feel there is no sense in ratifying a convention that does not apply here.
We are awaiting a legal opinion from the Minister of Justice with respect to convention No. 116 concerning the partial revision of the conventions adopted by the general conference of I.L.O. in 1961.
Is that an important convention?

We in the department look upon all the conventions as important because we regard the work of I.L.O. as important. If we do not agree that they are important we feel the time to say so is when they are being adopted. Canada has played an important part in many of these conventions, whether or not they are applicable to Canada.

Mr. Chairman, in my opinion this is one of the most important items that comes under the jurisdiction of the minister and so I should like to make some comments and ask some questions at this point. In my view we desperately need concentration on the entire problem of job training and should look for changing patterns of employment for the next 20 or 30 years. I hope to obtain some information in this regard under this item.
In support of my contention I wish to quote from the report of the special committee of the Senate on manpower and employment. At page 7 we find this statement:
It is essential that we keep the closest watch on changing patterns of employment, on the requirements for the various skills, on developments in foreign and domestic markets, on the effects of technological change, on the implications of changing levels of investment and changing patterns of government expenditure, on the impact of population growth, changing rates of family formation, and changing levels of immigration.
I realize that many of these areas of activity do not come within the purview of this branch of the department but certainly some of them do. The report goes on to say:
More specifically, steps should be taken immediately to initiate a continuous and comprehensive program designed to provide periodic analyses and forecasts of the size and composition of the labour force and the demand for workers in different industries, areas, occupations, and with different skills.
I note with some consternation that there are only five economists in the employ of this branch. This is a nation of some 18 million people with a labour force of several million persons. I am led to wonder if sufficient research is being conducted in the branch. I am aware that the people dealing with vocational training were very much concerned about the courses that were being set up. They want to know whether there is any point in training a welder. What will the employment opportunities be in five, six or 10 years from now? Is there any point in training a certain kind of pipefitter? Will this particular job disappear? I realize that in a sense this has all the appearance of star gazing and crystal ball gazing as well. Surely we have some bases on which we can operate. Surely we can send questionnaires to
Supply-Labour
employers and industrialists who to some extent know what the pattern of industry is going to be.
It seems to me that economists in the department might well spend their time looking at tables in the Labour Gazette and writing a few speeches and preparing reports to which the hon. member for Essex East has referred. I should like to know whether there are any long range research projects going on in the department having to do with this particular area and seeking out the labour problems over the next 10 to 20 years. If so, to what extent are they being carried out?

The hon. member for Peterborough quoted from page 7 of the report on manpower and employment. If he had looked at the paragraph immediately preceding the one he quoted he would have seen that the committee said:
The committee is impressed with the work being carried out in various branches of the federal government.
This of course included the Department of Labour, because the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour made a number of comprehensive submissions to this committee which helped it a great deal in the study it was carrying on.
As far as the recommendations in paragraph 2 are concerned, to which the hon. member has drawn our attention, I can assure him that we are going to do everything possible to live up to the request that has been made in this recommendation.

I am glad to hear that. Is any research project being carried out right now to try to give the employment picture of the future? I have in mind those who are setting up vocational courses for the unemployed in the various municipalities. Is there any possibility of carrying on these studies within the research branch? This is a question which I have thrown at me quite often by those who are operating in this area.

They are making this study continually, Mr. Chairman. In the particular field mentioned by the hon. member it would be of some help to those people who are engaged in the training if they knew what type of course they should undertake, and so forth. They can get all the help they possibly need and all the information they require as to the requirements of the labour force for certain skilled workers from our national employment service which has an up to date record in each and every district and area.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Labour
182.	Industrial relations activities including the administration of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, the Female Employees Equal Pay Act, the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act, the Annual Vacations Act, and regulations, and the promotion of labour-management co-operation, $643,798.

The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but my recollection is that in the speech from the throne two years ago, or some time since then, information was given of the government's intention to bring in amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Certainly if that is not so, the minister did during the course of the present parliament indicate the government's intention to bring forward other amendments to the act or a substitution therefor. We have not heard anything more about this intention. It seems to have suffered the fate of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and other well expressed intentions of this government such as providing a system of contributory pensions based on the United States experience. There is such a gap between good intention and realization that the minister will not mind if I inquire tonight what has happened to the proposed amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act?

My nature is tenacious and I like to finish whatever I am trying to do, in the best way I can possibly do so. My intentions with respect to this matter were certainly sincere and I asked labour and management to submit their recommendations and ideas as to what type of amendment should be made to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. This was done in 1958. It took quite some time before the various organizations, labour, industry, industrial organizations and business organizations were able to submit their suggestions. I will be quite frank with the hon. gentleman. I do not know what other course the hon. gentleman would have followed, but I found that management did offer many drastic suggestions affecting labour. On the other hand, labour had very few suggestions. They felt well satisfied with the present act. Under those circumstances I felt that since I did not have a balanced number of suggestions, one offsetting the other, I would not proceed with any changes in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act because one segment of the people who are affected by this act seem to be quite satisfied with the act as it stands now.

The minister's statement is an interesting one. I do not suppose there has ever been a finer tribute paid to the perspicacity and the vision of

Mr. Mackenzie King than the statement we have just had from the Minister of Labour. Mr. King was the first Canadian deputy minister of labour and then minister of labour. He played a significant role in labour-management relations. He was the author of this act. That it has withstood the chill blasts of cold winters subsequent to its introduction, is I think an effective and deserving tribute to a man who played such a great part in our national life.

May I just make a comment in answer to that. Those amendments are still under consideration and the time may arrive when we might amend this act. In view of what the hon. member said, namely that a great deal of credit must go to Mr. King, I must remind the hon. member that the original act has been amended many times so that it is in its perfect form now.

By a Liberal government. I should like to ask the minister a speculative question on this subject. The minister said he was still considering the possibilities of certain amendments. Does the minister think he is apt in this slow motion race to reach the post before the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration does with the famous revisions of the Immigration Act?

I realize the humour that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is endowed with and that he must display it at times; otherwise he might burst at the seams. I have given the reasons why. It is not on account of lack of activity on my part but because of the legitimate reasons I have given, and I was quite frank about them.
I am glad the minister recognizes that there is a difference between the legitimate reasons he has given and the reasons his colleagues give.
I do not make that comparison at all.

I should like to say one word. May I perhaps be so impudent or imprudent as to say that Mackenzie King and R. B. Bennett have been dead for a long while and all honour to their names, but let us now discuss and decide the problems of Canada in the light of conditions in 1961.

I feel sure that the government in its planning, although we have heard little about it since last December, had in mind some connection between the Department of Labour and the productivity council. When we are considering vote No. 182 having to do with fair wages, hours of labour and so on, I would think that there is a relationship, and perhaps the minister might tell us what

is happening with respect to the productivity-council which was talked about last December.
I said this afternoon that the productivity council will be meeting on Monday and Tuesday, September 25 and 26, to discuss subjects related to the matter which the hon. member has brought up.
Which would include hours of work.
Labour-management co-operation.
Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce be back to meet the productivity council?

Mr. Chairman, I recognize that what I wish to say is essentially related to the national employment service but I feel the matter is also of particular concern in connection with the progress that has been made in Canada under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and other labour legislation. I have reference to the possibility of employers using the national employment service to break strikes. An employer goes to the national employment service to get persons whom he wishes to employ in place of those who are on strike. The minister is quite right that the form which the prospective employee receives has the notation stamped on it that he is going to a strikebound plant or to a hotel such as the Royal York, but when a person has been unemployed for many months it is very hard for him to put the labour situation in Canada ahead of the welfare of his own family.
I think this has become a very dangerous precedent and a strikebreaking technique which has all kinds of implications. In my view the whole idea of a strike is that both sides suffer. The employer suffers through not being able to make a profit and the employee suffers through not having his wages. I think the unfortunate practice to which I have just referred has been aggravated as a result of the great unemployment in the last year. I should like to know whether the minister does not feel that some method should be devised whereby a plant where the workers are on strike could be considered as being out of bounds and isolated from normal labour procedures so that the national employment service would not be put in the position of sending people to a strikebound plant to the detriment of the striking employees. I would hope the minister might consider that as a possibility.

The hon. member realizes, I am sure, as he has admitted, that the national employment service has been set up to serve the public of Canada and that includes employers and employees. We cannot take sides
Supply-Labour
in these matters. The service has to perform the function for which it was established. 186.	To carry out the purposes of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act and agreements made thereunder, including authority, notwithstanding section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, to make commitments for the current fiscal year not to exceed a total of $27,108,700-payments to the provinces, $26,600,000.

This particular vote, I think, is of a great deal of importance. It is one of the most important items put forward by the Minister of Labour, but one which I am afraid has caused a great deal of consternation in many parts of this country. It involves, as well as the building of technical institutes and so on, the training of the unemployed. I cannot help but feel that this plan has been less than successful over the last number of months. It seems there has been no pattern set up whereby the local municipality really has any sense of confidence in what it is doing.
On June 9, I asked the Department of Labour just how many municipalities in Ontario had instituted programs for the training of unemployed persons under schedule M. I was informed that only five in the whole of Ontario had done so since April 1, 1961, namely, Brantford, Cornwall, Toronto, St. Catharines and Windsor. When one looks at the courses that are given in each of these centres, one cannot but notice the absence of any kind of pattern. Perhaps this is what I was trying to get at when I was referring to the department of research. I do not feel these people on the local level really know what jobs are going to be available in the future and therefore they are rather reticent about dealing with the problem. The hon. member for Essex East brought up the whole problem of academic training which must go along with this.
The municipality which I represent made a magnificent effort to retrain the unemployed, but this problem came up again and again. Another problem which arose, of course, was that of getting the unemployed into these courses. It seems to me that after the last war we developed a very worth-while system intended to help the veteran find the slot in which he could be placed after he was taken out of the service. I am not sure but what the Department of Veterans Affairs could be of great use in this particular area. It seems to me that surely there could be some counselling service in the national employment
Supply-Labour
office in these municipalities to bring about this kind of program. In Peterborough, they sent out questionnaires to all the unemployed, but then they faced the problem of getting the questionnaires back. The unemployed person has no knowledge of his abilities or the direction in which he should be going. You have, therefore, as many courses as you have people asking for them.
I realize that to a large extent this is a provincial problem but I feel that perhaps the federal government needs to take more responsibility by giving some aid to the municipality which is trying to provide this kind of retraining. One of the questions which I should like to ask is, have municipalities within all the provinces set up retraining schemes for the unemployed since the schedule came into effect in April, 1961?

The hon. member said that this problem lies within provincial jurisdiction, and it is one which is more jealously guarded by the provinces than any other. Consequently, it is not our intention to move in on this jurisdiction in any way whatever. All we are trying to do is to help the provinces advance an area of education for the training of certain types of people for whom we feel there is a need in Canada. We have agreements with all the provinces, the whole ten, in respect of this matter.
As an incentive to undertake these courses we raised these contributions from 50 per cent to 75 per cent of the total cost. That includes equipment that is necessary for these courses. This is as far as we go with respect to the direction. There is no direction from us at all. We extend help to these local people- boards of education or whoever they may be- who might be setting up these courses; and in guiding people as to the type of courses through our national employment service offices. That is where the employers put in their orders and that is where they are able to say, "In this area we can place immediately 12 welders", or five barbers, or three hairdressers, or whatever it may be. There is no sense in training people if there is no call for that type of trade in that area. If there is a call in another area, then we will most certainly direct them to that job after the training course is over.
I do not want to take up the time of the committee to explain this. However, last fall we were advised by the pipe line contractors that they had plans for the construction of many miles of gas lines in the province of Alberta, that this work would require specialized welders in this field and that we did not have that type of skill here in Canada in sufficient numbers to fill these jobs. We immediately contacted the three prairie provinces and with their co-operation and that of

Supply-Labour
the pipe line contractors who supplied the equipment, we were able to train sufficient specialized welders to fill the needs of these pipe line contractors for this year. Consequently, this is planning not in the socialistic way as the hon. member would have it instituted in Canada but it is planning to take care of situations. This is what we are doing and this is what we have done with good results.

Under this item I should like to commend the minister and the government for what is being done in technical and vocational training assistance. This financial assistance can very readily be seen in the details of payments to the provinces as listed at pages 264 and 265 of the blue book. I will just read two or three of the items:
Assistance to trade and vocational schools, technical institutes, and technical and vocational high schools: Capital assistance, $14,775,000.
Assistance towards operational costs of trade and vocational schools and technical institutes, $3,125,000.
Assistance towards operational costs of technical and vocational high schools, $1,965,000.
Under the heading of "Assistance for Training Programs" we find the following:
Training for unemployed workers, $4,000,000.
That is under schedule M which was referred to a while ago.
I think this indicates very well how much the federal government is paying towards the technical institutes. In the terms of the technical and vocational training assistance bill that was passed earlier this session, the federal government pays 75 per cent of the capital costs of these technical institutes and also of the equipment needed in these institutes. This is a very generous federal offer. As has been pointed out, it is inspired by Ottawa's conviction that much of our unemployment results from lack of training for many in Canada's labour force.
The city of Moose Jaw in my constituency has a fine technical institute built with federal financial assistance. The Minister of Labour was the guest speaker out there in January at the official opening of the institute. He was invited in recognition of the big part the federal government played in making the institute possible. The minister made a tour of inspection of the building. He knows that it was planned to accommodate technical and vocational classes until 1965 at least. He will be interested to know that the institute is already being used to capacity. In fact, it might now almost be described as being overcrowded. I have here figures in regard to training for schedule M, the special winter training for the unemployed. It indicates that more are being enrolled now than it had been

anticipated would be taking these classes, in 1965. On the grounds on which the institute is built there is room to double the size of the building. I suggest that this expansion should be undertaken as soon as possible, by next year at the very latest.
In his statement in the house last December the minister said that the success of any vocational or training program depends upon the supply of qualified instructors. I am sure that all in this committee will agree with this statement. The Moose Jaw institute has qualified instructors. What the institute needs is greater space for classrooms and workshops. I am drawing this matter to the minister's attention, although I know the initiative with regard to expansion must come from the provincial government in Regina. The Saskatchewan government has indicated that it is considering enlarging the Moose Jaw institute. I hope the minister will encourage the provincial government to undertake this needed expansion as soon as possible.

May I ask the minister whether he will be good enough to give us a breakdown by provinces of the money spent under this item during the last five years. At the same time I should like to know under what item we would get information with regard to the winter works program and unemployment assistance. In 1960 I asked in the house a question about the winter works program and I was answered by the Department of Labour. I later asked some questions about unemployment assistance and the answer came back from the Department of Labour. I have been looking everywhere in these estimates but I do not find anything that relates to this winter works program or to unemployment assistance. I should be greatly interested in knowing the amounts paid to each province during the last five years so that we could get a clear picture of how much money has been given away by the government to each province, in order to prove that since 1960 when the Liberal regime came into power in Quebec, they did much more to help with the problem of unemployment in the province of Quebec than did the previous government which declared that unemployment was not any part of its responsibility. The new regime in Quebec decided that it was a responsibility not only of the federal government and of the provincial government but of the municipal governments and of every person who wants to see his neighbour have some work in Canada.

I cannot read all these figures but I shall be glad to table them for the information of the hon. member. They go

back to 1957. These tables give the capital and operating costs for each province for vocational training.

The hon. member always says: you should have done this, or you should have done that. Hon. gentlemen opposite including the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence who intervened a moment ago, should know the answer in advance. The fact is that his colleagues are in office. It is they who are confronted with this terrific problem of unemployment. One of the ways of meeting that problem is to provide people with the necessary training so that they can assume jobs for which they are not at present fitted. But to demonstrate the inadequacy of the program, and in support of what has been said by the hon. member for Peterborough, let me recall what I said yesterday, namely that more than 2,600 applicants representing 70 per cent of the total applicants for vocational training in Toronto were rejected, because they did not have the necessary foundation to take the training which was being made available under this arrangement between the federal and provincial governments. How can a scheme be said to be meeting the problem, when more than 70 per cent of the applicants are said not to possess the qualifications necessary before the training can be undertaken? That is what the hon. member was seeking to establish. We are not going to make a real contribution toward the solution of the unemployment problem until we recognize the necessity of providing those

who lack these skills with the opportunity to acquire them. It is true that the administration of this program is something which comes within the authority of the provinces, but it is the federal government which provides 75 per cent of the capital cost, and surely in any agreement this government makes with the provinces it ought to be possible for the government at least to use its persuasive powers-its good offices-to see that the administration in the provinces is carried on in such a way as to meet the objective which the federal government and, I am sure, the provinces themselves have in mind.
This is what the hon. member is seeking to establish. I am sure that from my own interest in this problem-and I am not speaking now, politically, because this is too important a matter for that-I would welcome anything that could be done to make this program work more effectively. We cannot sit back and pretend we have solved the problem merely by voting money to the provinces to enable them to carry on certain projects. That is an important contribution, it is true, but we must go further and see that our people are provided with the facilities for training in all sorts of jobs-jobs in television and in many branches of electronics, for example. They must not only be given a basic training, let us say, in electronics, but training must be given to them so that they can appreciate the nature of the more advanced training they are to be given. There are all kinds of private schools in this country engaged in teaching people electronics. That is all to the good, but there is a responsibility which rests on this government and on provincial governments. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to solve this problem of unemployment this is one of the ways by which it could be done.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: The silliness we have just heard from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate is in line with what we hear all the time. His arguments have no foundation at all. maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Anybody who has paid any attention to my career in public life in this house, either on the other side or on this side, knows that there is no hon. member more concerned about saving the taxpayers' money than I am. I have not advocated extravagant courses, but we in the Liberal party think it is not extravagant to train the unemployed so they can earn their livings. It is a great deal cheaper to do that than it is to be paying relief and unemployment insurance when these men might better be working and adding to the productive wealth of the country. That is why I say in this particular instance that the greatest incentive you can give to the provincial governments and municipalities to do a good job in this field is to pay the whole cost in respect of those persons who are unemployed and being trained under this scheme.

This item provides also for the national employment offices, which are included in the offices of the unemployment insurance commission, so I should like to speak on the subject for a few minutes. I intended to speak on item 1, but I did not want to delay the estimates. I point out that while governments at the federal, provincial and municipal level do what is within their capacity financially to meet the unemployment situation, private business fails to accept its responsibility in many aspects in this country. I have seen numerous illustrations of this. They reap the profits and then leave the

governments to bind up the wounds of the industrial unemployment casualties, without accepting any responsibility whatever. Their decisions as to their operations are not related to the national interest or to needs of the employees but are, generally speaking, related to the rate of profit, the development of automation and also, because they are under the control of international cartels, are related to various monopolies in various fields. On the whole, they accept no responsibility to the state or to the workers concerned.
If I may illustrate, Mr. Chairman, I would say I received a letter today from the unemployed workers of Windsor. It points out that the automobile companies are laying off workers and at the same time going in for overtime. I am not going to deal with that because I know the hon. member for Essex East is very interested in that problem and intends to deal with it. Then, we have the illustration of the Canadian Pacific Railway on many branch lines in Canada, particularly the Kettle Valley Railway, reducing the service to the area from which they get their greatest profit without any regard for the employees or the circumstances that exist or the welfare of the district concerned. The government also knows that prominent coal mining interests in the maritimes have not played the game, not accepted their responsibilities so far as meeting the present circumstances are concerned. They have failed to co-operate with this government to do what they could to continue employing persons who are at the present time being laid off for the reasons I have mentioned.
Then, I come to the question of Algoma Steel. I want to mention this as an illustration particularly of how international cartels are frustrating government intentions. You get this under a capitalist society. I want to quote briefly from a book entitled, "The Power and the Money", by F. W. Park. I should like to quote particularly from the chapter headed "Shifting Patterns of Power".
Dosco, the other major steel producer acquired by the Roe group, has had a long and enormously complicated history. Inefficient management, bitter opposition to the demands of labour have characterized its past. Since the war it expanded under the presidency of L. A. Forsythe, Montreal lawyer. Forsythe died on January 1, 1957, and soon thereafter rumours began to circulate that other interests were seeking control. Dosco owns "almost unlimited" iron ore reserves at Wabana, Newfoundland, and Cape Breton coal; its Sydney steel mill is strategically situated for export markets.
The first stage in the bringing together of this new steel alliance was the purchase of Algoma through an intricate series of operations that show how quickly international groups of financiers and industrialists can combine for common profit and how little attention is paid in this process to any concept of national interest.

Some $60 million in cash was needed to buy a substantial block of Algoma shares from the Dunn estate. Here two new groups enter the scene in alliance with A. V. Roe of Canada. First is the West German firm of Mannesmann A. G. headed by Wilhelm Zangen, the other is the group controlling the McIntyre Porcupine gold mining interests. Mannesmann, as will appear, put up some $24 million, and McIntyre Porcupine between $12 and $13 million. The balance was supplied by the Roe interests and the Royal Bank of Canada.
Then, they go on to deal with the international investments of these various companies in countries in Europe, South America and other places.
The Mannesmann firm was established in 1885. By 1938 it employed 50,000 workers and owned coal mines, iron mines, smelter and rolling mills, with a distribution network that extended from Germany to Argentina .. .
Zangen, head of Mannesmann since 1934, was one of the executive council of WASAG, the Nazi munitions trust, along with Krupp, Stinnes, Vogler and Poenagen. A member of the Nazi party and of the SS, he was one of the group of big German industrialists who financed the Nazi rise to power and provided the armaments for Hitler's conquests.

I thank you very much for your consideration, Mr. Chairman, but I did want to bring this point out. We criticize the government, whether it is the federal, provincial or municipal government, but under our present system the government is not entirely in control of this particular situation. Here are these large monopolies and corporations receiving the benefit of Canadian funds and reinvesting their profits in other countries while we have natural resources undeveloped and workers unemployed. I just want to make this point. The point of view of the party to which I belong is that the only remedy is in some effort at planning by the persons who are responsible either directly to the parliament of Canada or the legislatures of the provinces. We are told there has to be planning to provide control of natural resources and their development, for the manufacture of a greater proportion of our raw materials in Canada instead of shipping them out of the country to such an extent as is done today. If you control the sources of energy, such as electrical power, then add to that the control of the raw material, then you can get federal-provincial co-operation to give the impetus to get this country moving in the direction where the governments elected by the people are going to do something to meet the unemployment situation.
I just rise to make these few observations because I am confident that, regardless of the best intentions of the government, under the present circumstances we must grasp this nettle with both hands and ensure that the parliament of Canada governs for the people of Canada and is not going to continue to govern for those interests who have no respect for the national interests or the people of this country under these circumstances.

I should like to ask the Minister of Labour whether consideration has been given to bringing farm labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act. The minister will recall that I have brought this problem of our farmers to his attention on previous occasions. I am sure this problem of ours will get worse before it gets better. With the

Supply-Labour
advent of automation on the farm, the farmer finds it difficult to find labour skilful enough to operate the highly mechanized implements he needs at the present time. Unless attention is given to this problem and a solution is arrived at, namely that of bringing farm labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act, it is my opinion that the farmer will suffer severely.
From past experience I know that when harvest time comes along, farmers are not able to get operators who are able to run these implements. They are able to obtain employment somewhere else where skilled labour is required and where, when they are not employed the whole year around, they are under the Unemployment Insurance Act. This is not the case with the farm labour. I would seriously request the minister to take this matter into consideration when the Unemployment Insurance Act is revised or amended.

speechtext:
I wish to raise a matter which the hon. member for Niagara Falls and
I	have brought to the attention of the minister on two or three occasions. On April 24 last, a number of unemployed came here to Ottawa in order to present a brief to the government. Those in our area-and I cannot give the exact number although I think it is
II	or 12-were disqualified as to unemployment insurance benefits while they were here in Ottawa. They were disqualified by a local official of the unemployment insurance commission. The reason given was that they were unavailable for work on that day. An appeal was taken to the board of referees which met in St. Catharines, and there was a split decision. Two members of the board voted to disallow the appeal and one voted to allow it. Those voting to disallow the appeal asserted that the men should not have their appeal allowed because they were not available for work on that day. The one who gave the minority report asserted that he thought they had fulfilled their obligation by reporting to the office that they were going to be away and gave the reason therefor. When that appeal failed, the men appealed to the umpire and the case was scheduled to be heard last Monday, but up until now I have not heard what decision there has been. I think it should be the inalienable right of all citizens to come here and make a presentation to the government without penalty. I think this is the very basis of our democracy. In reading over the evidence, I think I can say it was agreed that these men were honest, that they said openly in the office in Welland why they were coming to Ottawa and that they did not try to hide the facts in any way. Unfortunately for them, however, April 24 was the date on which they were obliged to report to the office and, according to them, sign in at the office. I do not

know exactly what that means. I know of a number of other unemployed who were here and probably they did not have to sign in on that day. I know that a number of unemployed were here from Windsor, Hamilton, Toronto, Oshawa and Peterborough; and to my knowledge not one of the other unemployed from those centres has had a disallowance of his unemployment insurance benefits. If I may give my lay opinion, I would say that the government is labouring too much the argument with regard to these men being unavailable for work when, in fact, there was no work for them. I do not find any criticism of the board of referees because they were giving their decision within the context and the ambit of the regulations. Injustice can result, however, because of lack of foresight and because of lack of ingenuity on the part of man to anticipate all the complexities for which he must provide in the regulations and in the statutes. Since we have been here in Ottawa, I think we have seen examples with respect to the statutes. In fact, it is said that the fathers of confederation could not foresee everything that has happened in order to include it in the British North America Act. If we cannot include everything in the statutes how can we include everything in the regulations when we do not pay as much attention to the regulations?
In my opinion there has been injustice here. I think too much emphasis has been given to the consideration of whether or not these men were available for work. The unemployment insurance commission in Welland did not call their homes or did not try to get in touch with them on that particular day. I think that the department here should be a little more humane and should use common sense. Had they done so, I think this matter could have been cleared up a long time ago.
