I just want to take one minute of the committee's time. First I want to support the request made by my colleague from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador that Newfoundland be made a separate region as far as the administration of unemployment insurance is concerned. I do not wish to expand on that request. In his remarks he has given all the reasons for it and there is no need to repeat them here.
The other reason why I am on the floor is to ask the Minister of Labour or the unemployment insurance commission to make a special exception for dragger fishermen. I have in my riding a number of fishermen who leave Newfoundland and join a dragger fishing out of Nova Scotia. These people leave their homes in early January and are away practically the whole year. The vessel will go on refit perhaps in the summer months when the fishing is perhaps not so good, but

it is not possible for them to go to the expense of going home at that time. They therefore find other work or get on some other boat which is still fishing. But after being away for nine or ten months, around Christmas time they do feel an urge to join their families, like the rest of us. If they do they are penalized for leaving work voluntarily-they are disqualified under present regulations from coming home to see their families, and if some other operator happens to offer them another job on another dragger while they are home they are further disqualified. These people are not protected. They are not given any holidays under any legislation we have on the statute books, and the only chance they have of getting a holiday is to take one in this way. I think they should be entitled to special consideration and that some way should be found to avoid having to disqualify these people if they return to see their families after seven or eight months. I should like to see some system worked out so that they could rejoin their families after working for a certain period without being disqualified from receipt of unemployment benefits.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
I have a problem here which I should like to bring to the minister's attention. It concerns the payment of agents for making out unemployment insurance claims. At the present time, in many of the smaller townships and more remote areas the commission has appointed agents to handle the work rather than go to the expense of setting up offices. At times it has been very difficult to obtain suitable men to do this work and the difficulty has been accentuated by the fact that the department will only pay $1 per application. The agent in the area is required to return all correspondence and, nine times out of ten, to return the unemployment insurance book to the regional office, in respect of which he has to pay postage. Thus the agent makes approximately 75 cents per application. In many of the offices in the larger centres where accommodation is provided I am sure the cost per application would work out at a great deal more than $1.
I am unable to find out exactly how this figure of $1 has been arrived at. I presume the applications have been handled in some of the larger offices where everything is convenient and where the claimant is an English speaking person and the costs have been based on that. But in many of these rural areas it is a problem even to understand some of the applicants who come into the offices or homes of the agents. I feel all this should be taken into consideration and that in the circumstances the payment of $1 is not sufficient.
Supply-Labour
We have allocated over $33 million under this vote, and I feel that an increase in the payment made to agents is desirable. I have here a certain amount of correspondence, some of which relates in particular to the appointment of an agent in Golden, British Columbia. I would point out that if a man applied for benefit in Golden and if his application could not be dealt with locally he would have to make a return trip to the regional office which is 380 miles away. The round trip would cost approximately $19 and applicants for unemployment insurance are not in a position to pay out travelling expenses of this kind. So I say that some consideration should be given to increasing this payment. The department, in the correspondence I have received from them, simply says "no" and that is supposed to be final, but I think the question should be given further consideration at this time. The agents are doing a good job in the smaller centres and rendering a valuable service to the public, especially to those who are in the unfortunate position of being unemployed.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned that I had received some representations from a Windsor unemployed organization, and that I proposed to say something about them. He had spoken to me earlier about this matter. I indicated that I had received these representations and that I intended to bring them to the attention of parliament and the Minister of Labour.
These are representations made by this organization of unemployed in the city of Windsor. These representations have been addressed to the Minister of Labour in this government, to the minister of labour in the province of Ontario and to the federal and provincial members from the county of Essex. The representations include an allegation that in certain automobile plants, not only in Windsor, lay-offs have taken place in large numbers; that some of those lay-offs include skilled tradesmen and that they have taken place at a time when there has been a scheduling of an overtime program covering as much as from 16 to 30 hours and more a week, though many are unemployed. This is a matter which concerns the hon. gentleman not only in his capacity as minister, because it applies as well, to the General Motors plant in Oshawa. I am sure he would want this matter looked into. I bring this matter forward as a representative from the city concerned with this problem. I have no hesitation in saying that at a time when there is a high level of unemployment, although responsibility for meeting that situation rests

Supply-Labour
primarily, I believe, on governments a responsibility likewise rests on employers to see that they in turn are doing everything in their power, having in mind all the problems which confront them, to see that men and women are not unemployed. I think the Minister of Labour would want to be satisfied that people were not being left idle at a time when they could be put to work, particularly if there is a heavy scheduled program of overtime work.
I do believe a more conscious effort, on the part of some employers as well as by governments, could rectify this problem.
I hope the minister will take a look at this memorandum which I propose to discuss with him at the earliest possible moment in order to see what correction can be made in this situation.
Yesterday I put before the committee and, particularly, before the minister, what I believe is one of our major grievances on these estimates at this time. The minister spoke this afternoon. I missed a few moments of the early part of his statement. If he covered this matter then, I do, of course, acknowledge that I may be in error in repeating the matter tonight. But in the absence of an explanation, I want to reiterate that I believe this government treated this parliament with contempt when it announced the appointment of a royal commission to enquire into the Unemployment Insurance Act, shortly after we adjourned in the month of July.
I have no objection to the fullest examination being made of the Unemployment Insurance Act by those who are competent to make recommendations as to what changes should be made to make that act more effective; nor have I any objection to anyone outside of this house indicating to us and to the government how the perilous state of the unemployment insurance fund could be dealt with. I believe this problem is a responsibility of parliament, but primarily it is the responsibility of this government. I believe when the government turns over to a royal commission a matter of this sort, and particularly when it does so under the circumstances attending this situation, it leaves itself open to the indictment that it is transferring to a royal commission the examination of this problem, to escape its own responsibility, especially when we realize how long this problem has been before the government.
We have had recently tabled the latest report of the unemployment insurance advisory committee for the year ending March 31, 1961. This report bears close examination by hon. members of this committee. At page 1 the committee reports that the balance in the unemployment insurance fund as at March 31, 1961 was $184,685,000. The report goes
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
on to point out that by May, 1962 there will be nothing left in the fund if the present levels of unemployment or levels comparable thereto persist in the ensuing period. This is a very serious situation.
We have continually reminded the government, during the course of this session in particular, but also in other sessions, of the dangerous state of the fund. All hon. members know that in 1956 the fund stood at over $900 million. We are now told that at the end of the last fiscal year the fund was down to $184 million. The report points out that by May next there will be nothing left in the fund unless something is done to bolster it. We have repeatedly asked the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance what the government was going to do. We asked if the government was going to bolster the fund by increasing the contributions. We indicated that if this course were followed we, in the Liberal party, would consider it an unconscionable thing to do particularly in the light of the action taken by the government two years ago, when it increased the contributions from 25 per cent to 55 per cent, imposing this added burden on the employees and employers of our country at a time when there was no change in the pattern of benefits.
If the government proposes to resort to that formula once again it will certainly meet with very strong response from those in the Liberal party who opposed this remedy so vigorously two years ago. As we all well recall, it was the Liberal party and none other that took that course in the house when we levelled criticism against the government at that time.
The government has now referred this matter to a royal commission. The Prime Minister does not call it that; he said it was a committee. The reason the Prime Minister does not use the phrase "royal commission" is because he has understandably become somewhat sensitive to the criticism directed at his government, that it is a government of royal commissions. The fact is, as I indicated yesterday, this government has appointed no less than fourteen different royal commissions to deal with matters which could have been dealt with by the government. During its appeal to the people in 1957 and 1958 the government promised it would resolve the questions which were covered in the references to these royal commissions.
This is one question the government said it would resolve. It has now turned over to a royal commission the responsibility for investigating the problem. We do not know when a report will be made. The commission has

not yet begun its public hearings, which I believe are to begin some time in October. We have had no indication from the Minister of Labour as to when this commission will report. He will have an opportunity to give an indication with respect to that question this evening. We also have had no indication as to whether the report will be received early enough to permit the government to bring down legislation before we go to the people in a general election.
The government owes it to parliament and to the people of Canada, to state what its position is with regard to amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and with regard to what the government proposes to do to bolster the fund, particularly in view of the fact that in the previous session of 1959-60- not in the session that adjourned in the month of July-it asserted that it had definite views as to what amendments should be brought forward. The government indicated at that time that those amendments would be brought forward in legislation at the earliest possible moment.
When we met last November at the beginning of this session we were solemnly told in the speech from the throne by Her Majesty's representative that the government was going to bring down amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. During the course of this session various members of this party have asked the Minister of Labour to say when the legislation foreshadowed in the speech from the throne would be presented. The minister said these matters were under careful consideration and would be presented in due course.
I believe it was on March 9, during the course of debate that I suggested that the government had then had in its possession for some eight months a special study presented to it by the unemployment insurance commission, containing a whole series of recommended amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The minister did not deny that that was the case. The minister cannot say he did not have before him a carefully considered body of recommendations presented by the unemployment insurance commission, composed of experienced people specially endowed to deal with this problem.
As late as May 9 last the minister said in the house as reported at page 4555 of Hansard of that date:
-a careful study of the report of the advisory committee leads to only one conclusion, namely that the situation cannot be met simply by merely appropriating money through parliament to meet the payments from the fund. It is evident that what is required is a careful review of the act, something which we are undertaking with the
Supply-Labour
officials of the unemployment insurance commission and with others, with a view to incorporating amendments that will restore the full effectiveness of the scheme.
When asked if the amendments would be introduced this session he said "of course, they would." He acknowledged that this had been mentioned in the speech from the throne. Two days before we adjourned, I asked the minister when we were going to receive the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The minister's reply was that the matter was under study and that the government's policy would be announced in due course. There was no suggestion then that we were going to have a royal commission, that the government was going to shelve its responsibility, that the announcements in the speech from the throne were going to be thrown aside or that the government was going to ask someone vicariously to give consideration to a matter about which the government told us it had definite views. There was nothing of that sort at all. We were again told the policy of the government would be "announced in due course." We had the right to expect when we returned, as we have returned, that we would have those amendments before us, and that a committee of this house would be established for the purpose of studying the amendments.
It cannot be argued that the amendments are so complicated, so difficult, that they defy consideration by the House of Commons, because the whole Unemployment Insurance Act, introduced by Mackenzie King as the leader of the Liberal party in the dark days of the war was not referred to a royal commission. It was referred to a committee of this house. It was a committee of this house which considered the legislation and put it into such form as to make it properly presentable to the committee of the whole and later to the house itself for approval. This is the course that should now be followed. Instead, we adjourned on July 13; we went to our respective constituencies and on July 27 the Prime Minister announced the appointment of a royal commission, to do something which this government said it was ready to do in the month of January.
I say, Mr. Chairman, the course taken by the government and by the Prime Minister on July 27 amounts to nothing less than contemptuous treatment of parliament. This is not the first time this has been done. It was done by this government on several other occasions. We tried to get the report of the advisory committee to the unemployment insurance commission in June 1960. As I indicated yesterday, and I repeat now, because

Supply-Labour
the minister has not commented on this important phase of administration in his department, on the very last day of the session, when we asked whether there would be a tabling of the report of the advisory committee, we were told by the minister that it was not ready. And yet, before six o'clock, before we had prorogued, the report was clandestinely tabled under our procedures with the Clerk. Only late that night, and after we had prorogued, did we learn of the existence of the report and of its terms. That was also holding parliament in contempt. Now we have had a repetition of this by the reference of this matter to a royal commission, composed of worthy gentlemen, who have no electoral responsibility to the workers of this country, as we their elected representatives have. I say this government has dodged this issue.

speechtext: Nonsense.

speechtext:
My hon. friend says "nonsense". This is his conventional repartee to any indictment made against a government which he so blindly supports.
The fact is that, along with other members, the hon. gentleman was elected to consider measures of this kind. He was not elected to transfer that responsibility to others, who were not elected.
This government has appointed 14 royal commissions. It has reported on only two of them. I suspect we shall have no report on this one, until long after a federal election and then it will be the responsibility of a Liberal government to deal with the recommendations made to it by this commission.
This is a vital matter, Mr. Chairman, one which affects thousands of people in this country who have a financial stake in the unemployment insurance fund. This fund does not belong to this government. It does not belong to the people of Canada. In the main the unemployment insurance fund belongs to two classes of our people. In law or in any other way this government has no right-

My hon. friend and others may laugh. This is an important matter to the workers of our country. This government has treated this matter in a shameful way. I can hardly believe that the Minister of Labour was in any way a party to this devious practice. I

can hardly believe that the minister who looks at me so sympathetically now-

speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen may think that an undertaking given through the mouth of Her Majesty's representative may not be important, but under our system of government it is important. This government has disregarded this fact; it has thrown parliament aside. What does parliament matter? "As soon as the session is over we will relieve ourselves of this embarrassment; we will turn the matter over to a royal commission", said the government. The commission will not report until after the election. The government will be saved the embarrassment of doing something which it should have assumed. The government believes it got away with it in the Clark report. It hopes it will get away with it so far as the Unemployment Insurance Act is concerned.
If this is the policy of this government, then I am sure the Minister of Labour will conclude his estimates tonight on a very sour note. This government has failed to discharge a responsibility about which it made a commitment two years ago to the country. This parliament, the employers and the workers are no wiser now as to what kind of changes are going to be made to an act the benefit of which we all recognize, particularly at this time of unprecedented unemployment in our country.
Surely the minister cannot fail to reply, to give us the reasons for this devious course taken by a government that is not inexperienced in the art of device.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, once again I am going to occupy only a limited number of minutes of the time of this committee. I should like to remind the committee-and I am speaking now to both Liberal and Conservative members of the committee-that half a dozen or so years ago I noticed that there were over $900 million in the unemployment insurance fund and I said at that time

that if ever an. economic recession hit the nation what then appeared to be an immense amount of money might disappear overnight and the fund would be in danger or on the verge of bankruptcy. I can still hear, almost as if it were yesterday, the hoots and the catcalls that I received from both the Liberal and Conservative members of the house on ;hat occasion.
Now the Liberals are blaming the Conservatives because the fund has been depleted and is facing bankruptcy. However, by their lack of foresight the Liberals even yet are responsible for the economic difficulties facing this nation today. I regret that, despite the election promises, the Conservatives have been unable to remedy the situation. We have had supplementary budgets, baby budgets and regular budgets and I do not know how many new names we will invent for budgets, but I noted with pleasure the announcement of the Minister of Finance in his latest budget speech indicating a willingness on the part of the Conservative government of the day to make a loan to the unemployment insurance commission in order to ensure that the unemployed will be able to obtain their legitimate benefits as prescribed by the act.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he define their legitimate requirements?

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: I would define the legitimate requirements of a man who is willing and able to work as being a minimum basic standard of living in this day and age.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: What is it?

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: You know, Mr. Chairman, when my grandfather first came to this country-

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: -he was able to take a gun over one shoulder and an axe over the other and go out and make his livelihood from the raw resources of Canada. Today a man who is unemployed is no longer able to go out with a gun or an axe over his shoulder because the so-called free enterprise system is now denying him the right to make his own livelihood. He now has only one alternative and that is to go to some employer, some corporation that may have its head office in Accra, London or New Delhi and say, "All I have are my two hands, my brains and my brawn; I offer them to you", and the employer has the power to say whether these brains and brawn are going to be usefully employed.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Ridiculous.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
I regret that I was unable to precede the hon. member for Essex East because I would have made the same plea for the unemployed of Windsor. I believe the
Supply-Labour
situation is regrettable and must be corrected in view of the fact that many people are being paid for overtime work while at the same time others who should be employed and who were employed in the same industry remain unemployed.
I want to mention a matter in connection with the unemployment insurance commission. I can remember the time when the Liberal government introduced a plan to pay pensions to the physically handicapped. The hon. member for Essex East, and I give him marks for it, was the man who introduced that measure in the house. At that time I pleaded with the government of the day that in implementing this most desirable plan they should not superimpose new administrative machinery throughout Canada. The hon. member may have forgotten my plea at that time. I said that the administration ought to be tied in with the existing machinery.
What concerns me is that a man who is unemployed today is entitled to so many weeks of unemployment insurance benefits but at the expiry of that time he then has to go into an entirely new world if he has been unable to find employment. He has to go to the municipal office and apply for what we have now decided to call social security but which we used to call relief. Once again he has to go through all the red tape, all the administrative procedures, in order to qualify for relief. We have welfare plans and pension plans in Canada that astound me. They run into the dozens. We have pensions for the blind, pensions for the handicapped, unemployment insurance, pensions for this, pensions for that, welfare for this and welfare for that, each scheme with its own hierarchy of officialdom, administration and red tape.
It is time that we adopted a comprehensive, all-inclusive social security system. I see no reason why we should not. I notice that a number of our civil servants are looking askance at me. If we were able to extend the number of weeks during which an unemployed man is eligible for benefits, I see no reason why we should not be able to extend our unemployment insurance system to the point where a man and his dependents will be looked after until work is again found and he will not have to be kicked out and have to go to the city hall and beg for relief or social welfare.
I know that the minister may say immediately that this is an anti-union attitude. I know that for many years the unions of Canada insisted that the Unemployment Insurance Act should be an insurance act, and therefore the proposals I am now making would be in violation of that intent. But the Unemployment Insurance Act as it is now

Supply-Labour
administered no longer has much of an insurance feature about it. It is in effect a welfare measure and we should not allow the unemployed of Canada to be kicked out of one welfare agency into another.
I am very pleased to note that the Canadian labour congress and the major unions of Canada are now pleading with the federal government to recognize that any costs over and above reasonable unemployment insurance benefits should be met out of the consolidated revenue fund and that adequate amounts of money should be paid into the unemployment insurance fund to meet needs in excess of reasonable demands upon that fund. The day has arrived when we can no longer laugh about this matter because the people of Canada are becoming very cynical. A lot of Tories are laughing behind the curtains. That is fine and I accept it, but I forecast to the house at least half a dozen years ago that if an economic recession came the unemployment insurance fund would go broke, and it has gone broke. The government does not want to do anything about the matter except to lend the fund $125 million in order to tide over the evil day for one more year. In the budget speech the Minister of Finance announced that the government was making provision to that end.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: But at 5 per cent.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: There may be an interest rate attached to it as the hon. member for Essex East points out. What this government must realize is that unemployment, beyond that which can be reasonably expected, is the responsibility of the government and that responsibility should not be put on the Minister of Labour or the unemployment insurance fund. If they are going to make a welfare instrument out of the unemployment insurance fund, then they ought to go all the way and pay benefits to the man who is without a job until a job is again found for him.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS

It was not my intention to speak on these items but I listened with great interest a little earlier this evening to the remarks of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. I believe they are worthy of some comment. He suggested that we extend the payment of seasonal benefits only to fishermen from Newfoundland, and I must take exception to that. I would be the last one in this house to speak out against unemployment insurance or seasonal benefits for fishermen, especially those in Nova Scotia or those fishermen from Newfoundland. Some of our best fishermen and sea captains in Lunenburg come from Newfoundland. We hope to secure even more men from that source.

However, we must be realistic. Under the present system, these men come to Nova Scotia early in March or April and join our ships in that port. They remain until September or October and then return to their homes. Now, to extend their seasonal benefits would work a further hardship on the men who are left to man the ships. After all, we are speaking about unemployment and about methods of curing it. The extension of these seasonal benefits would not improve this situation. You cannot run a fishing vessel or a dragger without a full crew and when these men return to their homes, of necessity the ship must be tied up to the dock. This situation creates some unemployment.
I should like to suggest, therefore, that the minister give careful consideration to the proposal made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo before taking any action. We do not want to create unemployment; we want to do everything possible to keep everyone physically capable of working employed in Canada.

maintopic: OPERATING COSTS-TRAINING FOR OTHER GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Lunenburg has misunderstood what I requested. I did not request that they be granted seasonal benefits in September or at any other time. Under the law, they cannot get seasonal benefits until December 1. What I did say was that these fishermen leave their homes in Newfoundland early in the year, some time in February or March. They go to the mainland and are employed there on fishing vessels until nearly Christmas time. Having been away from their families for almost a year, and being human like everyone else, they want to spend some time with their families at Christmas. They get no holidays, and the only way they can get a holiday is to take one. They leave these ships voluntarily to go to Newfoundland to spend Christmas with their families. When they leave these ships voluntarily, they are disqualified from receiving benefits.
All I asked the minister was to find some way of avoiding the imposition of a penalty on these people because they have been absent from their families for such a long period, and this fact should be taken into account. They should not be penalized because they are forced to resort to this method in order to spend time with their families. I feel they deserve special recognition and they should not be disqualified when they apply for benefits in December.

The minister has had a rather successful inning. I am sure he would expect now to be given an opportunity to catch his breath.
In the remaining few moments of tonight's sitting, the minister should tell us what progress he has been able to make, since he last addressed himself to this question. That is the study he has now been making for over three years of the Clark report. The minister may recall that the Clark report was a document, which had been prepared by a professor of one of our universities at the instance of the government. That professor had been engaged to make an inquiry into the operation of the old age survivors scheme in the United States, which operates on a contributory basis. The provocation for that report arose out of a statement made in this House of Commons by the Prime Minister of Canada. As the minister may recall if he will search his memory with diligence, prior to the election of 1958 the Prime Minister solemnly told the House of Commons that he thought we should have a system of contributory old age security, modelled on the principles of the system in existence in the United States. In order to meet that objective he said that he had appointed a Professor Huson of the University of Western Ontario, and that the report was to be completed within four months. At the time great publicity was given to this announcement of the Prime Minister. However Professor Huson decided that he could not possibly make the report in four months and, as a result, he resigned from the assignment.

speechtext:
In his stead Professor Clark was appointed. He took some eight or nine months and then presented a rather monumental document, in two volumes. The minister was questioned about this document a year and a half ago in the estimates committee. He then gave evidence of great comprehension and understanding of the report. No one was convinced that he had not fully studied it. At the end of the presentation of his evidence before the committee, we were somewhat surprised to find that he was not in a position to announce government policy. However, as I say, he clearly established in our minds the impression that he had carefully studied this report and that there was no paragraph in the complicated recommendations and factual statements made by Professor Clark, that the minister did not understand. But since that time we have been told repeatedly in this house by the minister that he has not yet completed his study.
With great respect and having in mind the minister's heavy responsibilities, may I ask him this question. I realize that he suffers a particular disability latterly, when he has not been able to walk the streets in his own clothes. However, that fact should in no way be regarded as an excuse for his not having completed the study. May I therefore ask him now whether the study has been completed. Has he made any recommendations to his colleagues? Does the government have any idea of implementing that report in part or otherwise? If it proposes to implement the report, is it the government's intention to establish a parliamentary committee, so that we may consider the report and the government's recommendations, or is this simply another stall on the part of this government, one that has devised more impressive ways of stalling than has any of its predecessors?
We have shown great forbearance tonight. We have progressed in the passage of the minister's estimates largely because we wanted to deal with this problem. We sympathize with the minister. We realize that he is the most studious Minister of National Health and Welfare in the history of our country. He is one of the most studious ministers, but he is not one of those who acts with the greatest rapidity. We ask him to tell us tonight what the government is going to do about this report. Is it something that we should forget?

speechtext: However, I appreciate the kind gesture. The hon. member for Essex East has given the complete history of the Clark report and therefore I do not think that I need to go into it. I should like to assure him that I am an extremely slow but thorough reader. After I have read an article I sometimes must go back and study the more difficult points, those with depth and meaning. I admit that process takes me some time. However, I can assure the hon. member that I am giving deep study to this report. An interdepartmental committee has been studying it. I should not be too greatly surprised if before too long he were informed of the government's action.

speechtext:
We have left just four items in the Department of National Health and Welfare; we have the privy council items to pass-these were commenced the other day when the Prime Minister was speaking. We

have also the estimates under the heading of legislation which Mr. Speaker himself deals with, and these do not normally occupy much of the time of the committee. We have also the Department of National Revenue, the Department of Finance and 20 items left in the Department of Transport, estimates of which were before the committee earlier, besides the Department of Veterans Affairs. Those are the estimates we have to complete.
On the legislative side we have the resolution stage with regard to the sports council, followed by the bill; the bill in connection with the Pine Point Railway which will be back for consideration in committee of the whole house and for third reading, and the debate on the dominion-provincial tax collection arrangements. For tomorrow, by arrangement, we shall take the resolution stage of the fitness and amateur sport proposal. On its completion, if we do not take all day on it-
We won't.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-I think we shall take the estimates of the privy council, followed then by those four items in health and welfare, and, depending on the time available, we might make a start, or perhaps even complete, the estimates of the Department of National Revenue.
Business of the House
Some positive thinking there.

speechtext:
Whether or not we sit
Saturday I think we shall determine by noon tomorrow. We shall confer and see what the house would like to do. If we sit Saturday we might then find it possible to complete the business of the house by Thursday of next week. If we do not sit Saturday we might still finish by Thursday of next week. I do not know.

Perhaps the leader of the house would permit one question. It is true that an order of the house was made that the government could be assured of going into supply on Monday and Tuesday. Is it the intention of the government to complete the legislation at the beginning of next week before going on to estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is a very good question. But I should like to make an announcement concerning Monday tomorrow because, as I say, we are so close to the end it is a matter of adjustment and I shall be in a better position tomorrow to give that information.
